Build me a Claude Code mod called "ant-farm" that makes subagent work visible: a mission control for my subagents.

What it does
- While a turn runs, a slim band above my prompt shows elapsed time, subagents running vs done, and the estimated spend so far.
- /antfarm opens a side pane that is a mission control. A header: the mission's state in one line, a mission clock (T+12:04), counts of running, done and failed, total cost, total tokens, wall time, and a budget bar. Then one bordered card per running subagent, one to three across depending on the pane's width: its number and task, a status pill (WORKING, THINKING, WAITING, DONE, FAILED), its model, elapsed time, what it is doing right now (the tool it runs and what it touches), a sparkline of tokens per request, a progress bar, requests, tokens and estimated cost. Finished ones fold to one line each below.
- The status must be read from real events, never guessed: thinking and writing from the chunks of the subagent's own model requests, the tool from its tool calls, waiting from a permission ask on its tool, done and failed from its turn's end.
- An activity timeline under the cards: the last 80 things the subagents did, newest first, each on the mission clock with the subagent's number: starts, handoffs, tool calls, file edits, endings, tools that failed or were refused, warnings. Twelve rows by default, more on demand, foldable.
- An inspector: pressing inspect on a card (or its digit 1-9 while the pane has the keyboard) opens a panel with that subagent's details, live state, numbers and its own recent rows; n and p move between subagents, x closes.
- Each subagent gets a small pixel-art ant that walks while it works and stops when it is done. One ant colour per model. The card's border takes that colour, turns green for a moment when it finishes, red when it fails, then dims.
- Under 40 columns, draw one plain line per subagent instead of cards so nothing is lost.

What is new here
- Budget alarm: a budgetUsd setting, off (0) by default so a first heavy session never reads as over budget; the pane shows "No budget set - add one in /config". Once set, when the session estimate crosses it, show a toast and turn the budget mark amber; past 2x the budget, red. It only warns, never stops anything.
- ETA: once a running subagent has made 3 model requests, estimate its time left from its pace so far ("~1m left").
- Narrow terminals: if the pane cannot open (under 144 columns), show a compact list inside the band instead of nothing.

How it works
- Track subagents through the agent spawn and turn step events and count tokens per model request; watch their tool calls and permission verdicts without changing any of them, and keep the model stream passing through untouched.
- Estimate cost from a small built-in price table per model and mark every cost as an estimate (≈).
- Deterministic only: no model calls of its own.

Build rules
- Mods are new (Claude Code 2.1.287+). Use your plugin-authoring skill and read the types it points to before writing anything.
- Only do what is described here: no network calls and no reading files the mod does not need, unless this prompt says so.
- Write at least one test for the main behaviour and run `claude plugin validate` and `claude plugin test` until both pass.
- Load it in this session so I can try it, then take my changes in plain words.
- When I say it is good, install it so it loads in every session, and tell me where it lives and how to turn it off.
mods.readme:
# Ant Farm

Watch your subagents work, and what they cost, live.

## Install

```
/plugin install ant-farm --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

- **The band.** While a turn runs, a slim line above the prompt shows the
  elapsed time, how many subagents are running and done, and the session's
  spend so far. It stays while background subagents still run. Other mods'
  band lines keep drawing, above it, so a long ant list never pushes their
  buttons out of view.
- **The pane is a mission control.** `/antfarm` opens it (mid-turn too, and it
  adds nothing to the conversation). At the top: Bolt, the mission's state in
  one line (`Working · 3 running`, `Waiting · 1 held`, `All done · 4 agents`,
  `2 failed · 1 done`), the mission clock (`T+12:04`), the counts, the
  subagents' total (price-table estimate), the session's spend against your
  budget (Claude Code's estimate where it keeps one) and a budget bar. With no
  subagents yet, Bolt naps here.
- **The cards.** One bordered card per running subagent, one to three across
  depending on the pane's width. Each shows its number and task, its ant,
  model and elapsed time, a status line (`WORKING · Bash npm test · 4s`,
  `THINKING · 12s`, `WAITING · permission for Bash`), a sparkline of tokens
  per request, requests and tokens, a progress bar, its estimated cost and
  ETA, and on a wide card how many tools it called, files it edited and calls
  that failed. The border takes the model's colour, green for a moment when it
  finishes, red when it fails, then rests dim. The pointer lights a card.
- **The status is read, never guessed.** `THINKING` while a thinking block
  streams in its own model request, `WORKING` while it writes or runs a tool
  (the status line names the tool and what it touches: `Bash npm test`,
  `Edit auth.ts`), `WAITING` while Claude Code asks you for a permission on
  its tool, or its agent list says it is held, `DONE` and `FAILED` at its end.
  A held subagent counts as waiting, not as running too.
- **The activity timeline.** Under the cards, the last 80 things the subagents
  did, newest first on the mission clock: starts and handoffs (`from #1`),
  tool calls, edits, endings with their duration, tools that failed or were
  refused, responses that hit a limit, the budget alarm. 12 rows by default,
  `+N more` shows 40, `hide` folds it.
- **The inspector.** `open` on a card (or its number) opens a panel with the
  subagent's task, type, model, start, where it came from, its live state, its
  numbers, a longer sparkline and its own last rows; `previous`, `next` and
  `close` move between subagents.
- **Keys.** While the pane holds the keyboard (ctrl+x tab, or a click into it)
  a subagent's number 1 to 9 opens it, `n` and `p` move, `x` closes the
  inspector, `f` expands or collapses the finished list, `t` folds the
  timeline; a `Keys` line shows then. Esc hands the keyboard back.
- **The ants.** Every subagent gets a small pixel-art ant, one colour per
  model. It walks while its subagent works, stands still and dims when it is
  done, and lies on its back in the error colour if it failed.
- **ETA.** Once a running subagent has made 3 model requests, its card shows
  an estimate of the time left ("~1m left"). It uses the subagent's own pace
  (time per request so far) and how many requests finished subagents of the
  same type needed this session. With nothing finished yet, it assumes the
  subagent is halfway.
- **Opens itself where it fits, once.** When the first subagent starts on a
  surface that docks panes beside the transcript (the fullscreen terminal, the
  desktop app), the pane opens on its own, at most once a session and never
  after you closed it by hand. Under 144 columns the engine holds such a pane
  back, so the band lists the subagents instead (one line each, with a
  **Hide** button). `/antfarm` opens it any time, and asks the dock for room
  for two cards across.
- **Narrow panes.** Under 40 columns the pane draws one line per subagent, no
  borders or art, and a shorter timeline, so nothing is lost.
- **Two estimates.** The session's spend (the band, the pane's budget line,
  the footer mark, the status line and the alarm) is Claude Code's own
  estimate, the figure `/cost` shows, labelled "Claude Code's estimate". It is
  summed at list prices, so it is not your bill (a subscription does not pay
  it). Where Claude Code gives none, the price-table estimate stands in. Each
  subagent's cost is always the price-table estimate: Claude Code does not
  total cost per subagent. Every figure is marked `≈`.
- **Budget alarm.** Off until you set `budgetUsd` in `/config`. Then the
  mod's status line under the prompt shows the session's spend against it. When it reaches the budget you get a
  toast and the budget mark beside the prompt footer turns amber; at twice the
  budget, another toast and red. Each crossing toasts once, and lands on the
  timeline.
- `/clear` (or another session taking this one's place) starts the farm over,
  as it does `/cost`.

## Settings

Every setting has a default, so the notice at install about options not yet set is expected; change them in `/config`.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `budgetUsd` | `0` (off) | Session budget in US dollars for the alarm, compared against Claude Code's own cost estimate (else the price-table estimate). Off until you set one; the pane says so. It only warns, it never stops Claude. |

## What it can touch

- **Files:** none. **Processes:** none. **Network:** none.
- **Model calls:** none. Everything is counted from the usage the engine
  reports for each model request; nothing is sent anywhere.
- **Engine calls:** reads Claude Code's cost estimate for the session (after each
  model request and turn end), reads the session's agent list (to pick up a
  subagent that started before the mod loaded, to settle one that ended
  without saying so, and to see one the engine holds), opens and lists its own
  pane, sets its status line, shows toasts.
- **What it watches, without changing it:** the chunks of each subagent's
  model requests (which kind streams: thinking, text, a tool named), each
  subagent's tool calls (the tool and what it names: a file's name, a
  command's first line, a pattern) and the permission verdict on them. The
  stream, the call and the verdict pass through as the engine made them; the
  main loop's own tool calls are not recorded. Anything shaped like a
  credential in those words (a token, a `password=` value, a key in a URL) is
  replaced with `[REDACTED]` before the pane keeps or shows it.
- **Memory:** its counts live in session state and are gone when the session
  ends. Nothing is written to disk.

## Limits

- **Per-subagent costs are estimates.** They come from a small built-in table
  of Anthropic's published API list prices (cached 2026-10-06), marked with
  `≈`. The table cannot see fast mode, batch pricing, partner clouds (Bedrock,
  Vertex) or negotiated rates, and it prices every cache write at the 5-minute
  rate. A model missing from the table shows its tokens and a cost of `?`.
  The subagents' sum can therefore differ from Claude Code's estimate.
- **Claude Code's estimate is read after each model request and turn end**, so
  the alarm can trip one request after the real crossing. A resumed session's
  estimate includes its earlier runs, as `/cost` does.
- **The fallback estimate counts only model requests of a turn.** Side
  requests outside a turn (titles, safety checks) do not pass through
  `turn.step`, so when Claude Code gives no estimate the table's misses them.
- **The status line cannot be coloured.** Claude Code's plugin status line
  takes text only, so the amber and red of the alarm are drawn on the budget
  mark beside the prompt footer, the band and the pane header; the status line
  itself says "over budget" or "past 2x the budget".
- **The ETA is a heuristic.** Subagents do not announce how long they will
  take. Treat "~1m left" as a rough guide, most useful once a few subagents
  of the same type have finished.
- **The pane opens unasked only where it would be a sidebar.** On the
  terminal's main screen (no fullscreen layout) use `/antfarm`.
- **The band and the footer mark draw on the terminal and the desktop app**,
  the surfaces that have them. The pane draws wherever panes are placed.
- A subagent that runs in a remote cloud session (`isolation: 'remote'`,
  internal builds only) has no local loop: ant-farm sees it start but none of
  its requests, and cannot tell exactly when it ends.
- A background subagent stopped from outside may never report its end; the
  mod checks the engine's agent list about every 10 seconds and settles it
  from there. A running subagent that makes no request for 10 minutes (with no
  main turn running) stops the animation clock until it is heard from again.
- An interrupted subagent shows as failed (red, on its back): Claude Code
  reports an interrupt as an aborted turn, not a success.
- Caps: the pane lists 50 finished subagents one by one and counts the rest;
  past 200 subagents in a session the oldest finished ones leave the farm,
  and with them the subagents' header totals (Claude Code's session estimate is
  unaffected). The timeline keeps the last 80 rows; the long form shows 40.
- The live status is what the engine said last. A subagent the mod only found
  mid-run reads `WORKING` until its next request says more; after a code reload
  every running one does. A permission ask is seen when Claude Code asks you,
  not when a subagent merely plans a tool.
- Hotkeys act only while the pane holds the keyboard, as Claude Code keys every
  pane; from the prompt, click a card's `inspect` instead.
- Task descriptions, agent types and model names are drawn with escape
  sequences removed and other control characters shown as U+FFFD.
- Whether the pane may open on its own follows the surface that drew last;
  with a main-screen terminal and the desktop app both attached, that can be
  either.

## Built from a prompt

This mod was built from [the ant-farm prompt](../../prompts/ant-farm.md).

mods.prompt:
Build me a Claude Code mod called "cloakroom" that keeps my secrets (API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys) out of what Claude reads and out of my saved transcripts, while still letting local tools use the real values.

How it works
- When a secret would reach Claude (a tool result such as `cat .env`, a pasted prompt, an @-mentioned file, project instructions, any row added to the conversation), swap it for a ticket like [secret:STRIPE_SECRET_KEY#1]. Tickets are random per session: they must not be derivable from the value, and the same value gets the same ticket within a session.
- Keep the ticket-to-value map in memory only. Never write real values to disk, settings or the mod's store.
- At session start, learn the values of secret-named variables in the project's .env files (e.g. .env, .env.local; names containing KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, PASS, PWD, CREDENTIAL, DSN, PRIVATE), so even short or unusual passwords are caught.
- Once a value is known, hide it everywhere it appears later, exactly, including its base64, URL-encoded and JSON-escaped forms. This catches `echo` and `printenv` repeats that pattern matching misses.

Detection
- Known vendor key formats (AWS access keys and secret keys including ones that contain "/", GitHub, Anthropic, OpenAI, Stripe, Slack, Google, Twilio, Resend, SendGrid and similar), private key blocks, JWTs, Bearer and Basic auth headers, passwords inside connection URLs (including redis://:pw@), and long high-entropy strings next to a secret-like name.
- Do NOT hide: git SHAs, UUIDs, lockfile integrity hashes, git@host remotes, image names like logo@2x.png, version numbers, MAC addresses. Ship a test corpus of things to hide and things to keep.
- All patterns must run in linear time so hostile text cannot stall a check.

Where real values come back (the most important rule)
- Tickets turn back into real values only inside local tools: Write, Edit, NotebookEdit, and Bash when the command is proven local. Never in web fetches, MCP tools, subagent prompts, messages to other sessions or questions shown to me.
- A Bash command gets the real value only for a positive reason: every program on the line is on a short local-only list of text and file tools (echo, printf, cat, tee, cp, mkdir, grep and kin; heredoc bodies are data), and nothing on the line points at the network. Anything else is held with a red band and Allow once / Deny buttons, Deny focused: a network program (curl, wget, nc, ssh, scp, git push, bash's /dev/tcp, a remote URL beside the value) shows "held: STRIPE_SECRET_KEY#1 was about to leave via curl to paste.example"; a wrapper, interpreter, runner, script or variable as the program (sh -c, eval, node, python, npm, make, find, xargs to a shell) shows "held: STRIPE_SECRET_KEY#1 is in a command cloakroom cannot vouch for: sh is not on its local-only list". Never pass a command because no threat was recognised in it. Allow once lets that exact command run one time.
- If a tool input contains a ticket the mod no longer knows (for example after a restart), refuse the call with a clear message instead of writing the literal ticket into a file.
- Add one short line to Claude's instructions: hidden values appear as [secret:...] tickets; prefer referencing environment variables such as $STRIPE_SECRET_KEY in commands instead of literal values.

Fail closed
- If redaction throws or runs out of time, withhold the result and say so. Never let unscanned text through.
- Always hand back a fresh result object so the redacted text is what Claude actually reads.

Commands
- /cloakroom lists this session's tickets: name, kind, where it came from, how often used. Never the value.
- /cloakroom show <ticket> displays the value to me only (never to Claude). /cloakroom forget <ticket>.
- /cloakroom audit scans my past Claude Code transcripts on this machine (read-only) for keys that were already exposed, and lists which ones to rotate, by kind and date, without printing the full values. The list is drawn in a pane on my screen, never in the command's output, which Claude reads.

Be honest in the README
- Lead with what it can and cannot do. It CAN keep secrets out of the model request, transcripts, screen shares and exports at every door it hooks, and hold commands that would carry a known secret off the machine. It CANNOT stop a malicious mod installed alongside it, settings hooks, a command like `printenv | curl` whose value never enters the conversation (it can only hold the command if it sees it), images, or exposure that already happened. Never claim it "prevents exfiltration".
- Permission dialogs may show a restored value in a Bash command; say so, and that preferring $VAR references avoids it.

Guardrails
- No network, no processes, no model calls. File reads only for .env files at start, @-mentions it scrubs, and transcripts during /cloakroom audit.

Build rules
- Mods are new (Claude Code 2.1.287+). Use your plugin-authoring skill and read the types it points to before writing anything.
- Only do what is described here: no network calls and no reading files the mod does not need, unless this prompt says so.
- Write at least one test for the main behaviour and run `claude plugin validate` and `claude plugin test` until both pass.
- Load it in this session so I can try it, then take my changes in plain words.
- When I say it is good, install it so it loads in every session, and tell me where it lives and how to turn it off.
mods.readme:
# Cloakroom

Check your secrets at the door. Claude gets a ticket; the real value only comes back where you allow it.

## What it can and cannot do

Read this first. Cloakroom lowers the chance that a secret ends up somewhere it should not. It does not make that impossible, and it never claims to prevent exfiltration.

**It CAN:**

- Keep secrets out of the model request, the saved transcript, screen shares and exports (all but Claude Code's own permission box, see the CANNOT list), at every door it hooks: tool results (every tool, MCP included), your prompt and pastes, `@`-mentioned files, CLAUDE.md and the first message's context, the system prompt's sections, reminders and settings-hook output, skill text, every row the conversation stores, messages to and from other agents and sessions, and records sent to your own OpenTelemetry collector. A secret becomes a ticket such as `[secret:STRIPE_SECRET_KEY#k3x9qa]`.
- Learn the secret-named values in your project's `.env` files when the session starts (those long and varied enough to be a real secret, see Limits), then hide them wherever they show up later, including their base64, URL-encoded and JSON-escaped forms. That catches an `echo` or `printenv` that no pattern would.
- Turn tickets back into real values only inside Write, Edit and NotebookEdit, and inside a Bash command made only of local file tools (see "Which Bash commands get the real value"), so Claude can still write your `.env`. Web fetches, MCP tools, subagent prompts, messages to other sessions and questions shown to you keep the ticket.
- Hold any other Bash command that carries a known secret until you press **Allow once**: one that names a network program (curl, wget, nc, ssh, scp, rsync to a remote, git push, bash's /dev/tcp, a remote URL beside the value), and one it cannot vouch for at all (`sh -c`, `bash -c`, `eval`, `source`, `node`, `python`, `npm`, `make`, `find`, `xargs` to a shell, a script, a variable used as the program). A hold needs a positive reason to pass, never the absence of a known threat.
- Find secrets already written into your past Claude Code transcripts (`/cloakroom audit`), so you know what to rotate. The findings are drawn in a pane on your screen, never sent to Claude.

**It CANNOT:**

- Stop a malicious mod installed beside it. A mod whose hooks run before cloakroom's sees values before they are hidden; one whose tool hooks run after it sees restored values.
- See into your settings hooks (`hooks` in settings.json). They receive tool inputs and outputs on their own path.
- Stop a secret that never enters the conversation. `printenv | curl ...`, a `$STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` reference, or a script that reads `.env` itself all pass: cloakroom only holds a command when it can see the value in it. That is also the recommended way to use a secret in a command, and Claude is told so.
- Tell where a local program's output goes once it is on disk. A value cloakroom wrote into `.env` with `echo` can be read and sent by the next command, which it checks on its own when the value is literal in it, and cannot when the command reads the file.
- Vouch for a local port. A command that hands a value to `curl http://localhost:3000` is held like any other network call, because a local port can forward anywhere.
- Tell a program by anything but its name. `./echo` or `/tmp/cat` is taken for the real `echo` or `cat`; a script that borrows a local tool's name is the same case as a script that reads `.env` itself.
- Read images, PDFs or other media. A key in a screenshot reaches Claude.
- Undo exposure that already happened. Rotate anything `/cloakroom audit` finds.
- Keep a restored value off your screen when Claude Code asks permission. The permission dialog shows a Bash command or file content after the ticket was swapped back. In auto mode, the permission classifier reads it too, and that is a model request. Writing `$STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` in commands instead of the value avoids both. Cloakroom tells Claude to prefer that.
- Remember anything across a restart. Tickets live in the mod's memory only, so a ticket from before a restart or reload is refused in tools rather than written as text. Paste the value again, or use its environment variable.

What the validator sees it reach (`claude plugin validate --strict`):

```
hooks: session.start, tool.call, prompt.submit, prompt.mention, prompt.attachment, prompt.context, prompt.compose, skill.prompt, session.append, session.send, session.receive, telemetry.log{to=collector}, ui.render{component=AbovePrompt}, ui.render{component=Pane, requestId=cloakroom-audit}, command.run{command=cloakroom}
answers its own command: command.run{command=cloakroom}
gating hook with .catch: tool.call, prompt.submit, prompt.mention, session.append, session.send, session.receive, telemetry.log{to=collector}
calls: $.clock.after (via show), $.clock.now, $.command.register, $.env.get, $.fs.exists, $.fs.list (via listDir), $.fs.read, $.fs.write, $.prompt.submit, $.session.surfaces (via audit, show), $.ui.invalidate (via redraw, rescanCached), $.ui.open (via audit), $.ui.resolve, $.ui.toast
env writes: nothing
env reads: CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, HOME, TEMP, TMP, TMPDIR, USERPROFILE
hooks telemetry for: collector
```

## Which Bash commands get the real value

A real value is swapped into a Bash command only when every program on the line is on this list, and nothing on the line points at the network:

`echo printf cat tee head tail wc uniq cut tr rev fold paste column grep egrep fgrep cmp diff comm jq test [ true false cp mv mkdir rmdir touch ls stat chmod chown ln readlink realpath basename dirname pwd cd date sleep base64 xxd od hexdump md5sum sha1sum sha256sum shasum`, plus the shell's own `export unset set local declare typeset readonly shift return break continue exit read wait umask`, and `if for while case` and the other shell keywords. Heredoc bodies are data. `sudo`, `env`, `timeout`, `nice` and `nohup` are looked through to the program they run.

Everything else is held with the red band, for example `sh -c '...'`, `eval`, `node -e`, `python -c`, `npm run`, `make`, `find`, `xargs ... sh`, `./script.sh`, `$PROGRAM ...`, `sed`, `awk` and `sort` (all three can run other programs), and any `curl`, `wget`, `nc`, `ssh`, `git push` or remote URL. The band names the program, Allow once runs that exact command one time, and Claude is told to prefer the variable (`$STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`), which passes untouched because it carries no value.

## Install

```
/plugin install cloakroom --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

There is nothing to turn on. From the next session, a secret that would reach Claude arrives as a ticket instead:

```
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=[secret:STRIPE_SECRET_KEY#k3x9qa]
```

The same value keeps the same ticket for the whole session. The random part is drawn fresh each session and never computed from the value. When you paste a key into a prompt, a short notice says it was swapped. Claude reads one added line in its instructions: tickets turn back into real values only in Write, Edit, NotebookEdit and Bash, and it should prefer environment variables in commands.

**The red band.** When a Bash command carries a secret and cloakroom cannot vouch for it, Claude is told the call was held, and a band appears above the prompt:

```
held: STRIPE_SECRET_KEY#k3x9qa was about to leave via curl to paste.example
Claude was told to wait. Allow once lets this exact command run one time.
[ Deny ]  [ Allow once ]
```

or, for a command that is not made of local file tools:

```
held: STRIPE_SECRET_KEY#k3x9qa is in a command cloakroom cannot vouch for: sh is not on its local-only list
```

Shell syntax it cannot follow is named as the feature it is, such as `process substitution <( ) can run a program`.

The band never takes the keyboard by itself. Click it, or press ctrl+x tab, and the focus starts on **Deny** (`d` also denies). **Allow once** has no key, so a stray keystroke cannot press it; click it or move to it on purpose. Allow once lets that exact command run one time within 10 minutes and tells Claude it may run it again. Deny leaves it refused. While a hold waits for you, it is drawn on its own (other mods' bands come back once you answer), so nothing another mod draws can hide Deny.

**Commands:**

- `/cloakroom` lists this session's tickets: the name, the kind, where it was found, and how often it was hidden and restored. It never prints a value. Like any command's output, the list is a transcript row that Claude reads; Claude already sees the tickets themselves.
- `/cloakroom show <ticket>` draws the value in the band above the prompt for 30 seconds, with a Hide button. It goes to your screen only, never into the transcript or to Claude. Control characters in a value show as U+FFFD.
- `/cloakroom forget <ticket>` stops hiding that value for the rest of the session (for a false positive). Its ticket stops working in tools.
- `/cloakroom audit` checks your past transcripts and lists each exposed secret by kind and date, with a preview such as `sk_live_...9f2`, in a pane on your screen only. Claude is told only that the results are in the pane: not a preview, name, date or file. Values under 16 characters show only their length. Run it again to continue past the time budget.

`show`, `forget` and `audit` run only when you type them (in the terminal, the desktop app or Remote Control). Another plugin, a peer session, a channel or a prompt-injected Claude running them is refused. The plain list runs from anywhere.

## Settings

None.

## What it can touch

- **Files read:** your project's `.env` and `.env.*` files at session start, at the root and up to two folder levels down (`apps/web/.env`), skipping `node_modules`, `.git`, build output and hidden folders, at most 120 folders. A file you `@`-mention, so it can be checked first. Your transcripts under `~/.claude/projects` (or `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/projects`), only when you run `/cloakroom audit`, newest first, at most 4 MiB per file and about 6 seconds and 96 MB per run.
- **Files written:** a copy of an `@`-mentioned file that held a secret, with tickets in place of the values, under `$TMPDIR/cloakroom-<id>/`. Claude reads that copy and is told the real path. Nothing else is written: no store, no settings, no plugin state. A real value is never written to disk by cloakroom.
- **Memory:** the ticket-to-value map and the last audit's results, in the mod's own memory, gone when the session ends or the mod reloads.
- **Shown to Claude:** the plain `/cloakroom` list and the one-line answers of `show`, `forget` and `audit`, as any command's output is. Never a value, and never the audit's findings.
- **Environment:** reads `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `HOME` and `USERPROFILE` (to find transcripts) and `TMPDIR`, `TEMP` and `TMP` (for mention copies). Writes none.
- **Prompts sent:** one, only after you press Allow once, telling Claude it may run the held command again.
- **Telemetry:** rewrites records bound for your own OpenTelemetry collector when one is configured. It never touches Anthropic's own analytics.
- **Network, processes, model calls:** none.

## Limits

- Detection is pattern-based: known key formats (AWS, GitHub, Anthropic, OpenAI, Stripe, Slack, Google, Twilio, Resend, SendGrid, Mailgun, npm, PyPI, GitLab, Hugging Face and more), private key blocks, JWTs, Bearer and Basic headers, passwords in connection URLs, and values written next to a secret-like name. A secret in an unknown format with no telling name can be missed. Stripe publishable keys (`pk_`) and documentation examples are left alone on purpose.
- Only a value that is at least 8 characters, varied enough (about 3 bits of entropy per character), not a filesystem path and not a common default (`postgres`, `password`, `admin`, `changeme`, `localhost` and the like) is learned and hidden everywhere it appears. A short or common-default value is not learned and is only caught by shape: `DB_PASSWORD=hunter2` is hidden where it sits next to its name, but the bare word `hunter2` later in a log is not, and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres` is left alone so `postgres` in image names, lockfiles and package lists stays readable. A path next to a password-like name (`PWD`, `OLDPWD`, `PASSWORD_STORE_DIR`) is never treated as a secret.
- Every pattern runs in linear time. A test sends 1 MB and 5 MB of text built to stall pattern matchers through a real tool call, best of three runs each, and requires the 5 MB run to take under 8 times as long as the 1 MB one (linear is about 5 times, quadratic 25), with a 15-second backstop (alone, 5 MB measured about 0.6 seconds on a laptop). Text over 16 MB, text whose check overruns 4 seconds, or a value nested too deep to walk is withheld rather than passed on unchecked.
- If a check fails, the text is withheld, not sent. A tool result becomes `[cloakroom: result withheld, redaction failed]`, a prompt is not sent (it says why), an `@`-file is not attached, and a call that could not be checked does not run.
- The band (holds and `show`) draws in the terminal and the desktop app. In VS Code and on mobile there is no band: a held command stays refused (run it yourself), and `show` says it needs one of the other two. So does `audit`, whose pane is drawn only there too.
- Some things are written by Claude Code itself, outside the doors cloakroom hooks: a large tool output it saves to its tool-results folder, and its own prompt history (what the up arrow recalls), which may keep a pasted key as you typed it.
- A row may flash on screen, or reach an SDK stream or Remote Control, just before cloakroom rewrites it. Neither the model nor the transcript file reads that form. Tool results are rewritten before they are drawn.
- Context another mod attaches to a tool result cannot be changed at that point (Claude Code requires it word for word). It is scrubbed when it reaches Claude, as an attachment and as a stored row.
- An `@`-mentioned file is read twice, once by cloakroom to check it and once by Claude Code, so a file changed in that instant could slip past the first check. The attachment is still scrubbed when it reaches Claude.
- `show` puts the value in the band. Another mod that draws around the band can read it there.

# Crossroads

Three ways forward after every turn, risky ones marked. About $0.0002 a turn.

```
1: run the auth tests · add the same guard to signup.ts · push to main (pushes) · 0: dismiss
```

## Install

```
/plugin install crossroads --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

- When Claude finishes a turn with an answer, a small band appears above your prompt with three specific next prompts. A dim row shows while they are being made.
- Each item is a button: click it to put that suggestion in your prompt as an editable draft. It is never sent for you. Press **0** to dismiss the list.
- **Crossroads gives its own suggestions no keyboard shortcut.** Every row it writes is click-only: no number key, never above Claude Code's own guess, never the ghost text. A stray key can never draft one of them. Earlier versions tried to privilege "clearly safe" suggestions with an allowlist, but no list of words reliably tells a safe next step from a risky one, so v1 does not try.
- Claude Code's own guess (the dim ghost text you take with Tab) is left exactly as Claude Code shows it. When there is one, it is option 1 in the list and the only row with a number key (**1**, in an empty prompt), since it is already one Tab away. So you never see two different "next" ideas.
- Risky suggestions also get an amber note such as `(deploys)`. The small model tags each suggestion it writes as risky or not, with a short reason, and keyword rules back that tag up (risky if either says so). Claude Code's own guess has no tag, so the keywords mark it. Letters dressed up to slip past (lookalikes from other alphabets mixed into a Latin word, fullwidth or styled letters, invisible or control characters) are marked `(unusual letters)`. This flags common risky actions; it is not exhaustive, so the note is information only and never grants or removes a shortcut. Russian, Ukrainian and Greek text is normal text and is never marked for its alphabet.
- If Claude's reply ends with numbered options, the number key is left alone for that turn so typing a number answers Claude. The items stay clickable.
- The list clears the moment you submit anything. It waits for background subagents to finish before suggesting.
- **Desktop app:** the desktop prompt box cannot be filled by a mod, so clicking an item copies it to your clipboard and shows a clearly labelled **Send this prompt now** button. **Close** comes first and is where the focus starts, so a stray Enter closes; Send is never the default and has no hotkey.

Commands:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/crossroads` | Today's calls and estimated cost, this project's counts, back-off state (shown as a toast; Claude never reads it) |
| `/crossroads off` / `on` | Turn the mod off or back on (off also stops judging Claude Code's own guess) |
| `/crossroads forget` | Wipe what it counted for this project |

## Settings

None. Use the commands above.

## What it can touch

- **Model calls:** one small-model call (`haiku`, low effort, capped at 1,200 output tokens and 20 seconds) per finished main-loop turn. If your setup refuses the `haiku` alias, it tries once more with the small model your environment names (see Reads), so at most two. Skipped on trivial turns (under four words, or no tool use and no question), on subagent, error and refusal turns, while backing off, and whenever neither the terminal nor the desktop app is attached to draw the band (a headless `-p` run, an SDK host, VS Code or mobile alone), so nothing is spent on a list nobody would see. Typical cost about $0.0002 at Claude Haiku 5.5 list prices; `/crossroads` shows today's estimate.
- **What is sent:** a compact digest, never the transcript: your first prompt (the goal), your last prompt, the names of files Claude edited or read (no paths, no contents), the first line of each command it ran with passed or failed, Claude's closing question, the names of up to 12 slash commands (those used in this session first, then the other installed ones that are not built in, such as plugin, skill and your own commands), your top three suggestion kinds, and Claude Code's own guess when there is one. Anything that looks like a secret (AWS, GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, Stripe, Slack, Google, Hugging Face, npm and Twilio keys, JWTs, private key blocks including PGP, Slack and Discord webhook URLs, `password=` style assignments such as `SECRET_KEY_BASE=` or `dbpass=`, secret flags such as `--password X` or `--token X`, `mysql -pX`, `curl -u user:pass`, bearer and `Authorization: token` headers, "my password is X", passwords in URLs) is replaced with `[REDACTED]` first.
- **Reads:** the session's transcript in memory, the slash command list, the `/config` rows (to see whether Claude Code's own suggestion is on), the subagent list, and two environment variables (`ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL`, `ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL`) used only if the `haiku` alias is refused, and the text in your prompt box when you press an item (so your draft is kept and the item goes after it). No files, no processes, no network.
- **Writes:** your prompt box (only when you press an item), your clipboard (desktop fallback), toasts (the `/crossroads` answers, which never enter Claude's context), and the plugin's own store: an on/off flag, today's call count and token totals, and per project (keyed by a hash of the project path) counts of the kinds of suggestion you took, edited or ignored. Never your prompts or the suggestions themselves.
- **Sends a prompt** only when you press Send in the desktop fallback. It goes in as your own words (`asUser`); the transcript still records that Crossroads submitted it.

## Limits

- In the desktop app, a `/crossroads` sent as the very first prompt of a new session may show "/crossroads isn't a command here." The app checks the command before mods have registered theirs; the command still runs, and later ones show no such line.
- The model's reply must be strict JSON followed by an `END` line. A reply that is cut off or malformed shows nothing rather than half a list.
- Claude Code's own guess only exists in the terminal, and only when its prompt suggestions are on. Crossroads waits up to 4 seconds for it, then writes all three itself. A guess that arrives later becomes option 1 (the last suggestion drops off), so the ghost text and option 1 still agree.
- Button labels keep the surface's own button style (the API gives buttons no colour), so the risk note beside a risky item is what is amber.
- Back-off: after 3 lists in a row are ignored or dismissed, a list comes every 2nd, then 4th, then 8th eligible turn, until you take or edit one.
- Numbered-option detection is a heuristic. A reply ending in a short numbered list of steps may also turn the number key off for that turn (the items stay clickable).
- If the `haiku` alias is refused and no provider model id is set in the environment, Crossroads says so once and makes no calls for the rest of the session.
- On the desktop app the copy may not reach your clipboard: this release of the mods API says remote surfaces have no clipboard path yet. The band then says it could not copy and shows the suggestion, and Send still works.
- The VS Code and mobile surfaces do not draw the band above the prompt, so Crossroads shows nothing there and makes no model call for them.
- Secret hiding works on shapes, not meaning: a secret with no recognisable prefix or name around it (a bare password repeated in Claude's closing question, say) can still pass through.
- The amber note flags common risky actions; it is not exhaustive. A risky suggestion the model does not tag and no keyword knows is shown with no note. It is still click-only, like every row Crossroads writes.
- Claude Code's own guess is not filtered: if it suggests something risky, it is still the ghost text and option 1 (with an amber note when the keywords know it). Read it before you press 1 or Tab.

# Fine Print

A second reader that flags what you would miss in a wall of text.

After a long reply, a small, cheap model reads it with a summary of the tool calls behind it. If there is something you must know (a hidden cost, a security or privacy risk, data loss, an action that cannot be undone, an effect on customers, or an assumption made without asking), a short note appears above your prompt. Otherwise it stays silent.

## Install

```
/plugin install fine-print --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

There is nothing to run. After any reply over 150 words, Fine Print checks it in the background, after the turn has ended.

When it finds something, a band appears above the prompt:

- a bold one-line headline and up to 4 bullets
- **Got it** (`g`): you read it; the band closes
- **Explain more** (click it, or Tab to it and Enter; it has no letter key, so a stray keystroke never sends a message): sends a follow-up question into the chat, so Claude explains the note in plain words. The question is sent as the Fine Print plugin's message, not as yours: the transcript and the model both see that the plugin wrote it, at your press. Claude's answer to it is not checked again.
- **Dismiss** (`d`): closes the band without marking it read

The letter keys (`g`, `d`) work once the band has focus (a click, or ctrl+x tab). A newer note replaces the one on screen; the band then says how many older notes are still open.

`/fineprint` opens a pane (also while Claude is working; Esc closes it) listing every note flagged this session, newest first, with what you did with it (open, got it, dismissed, asked to explain), how long ago, its topics, and how many checks were used.

## Settings

Every setting has a default, so the notice at install about options not yet set is expected. Change them in `/config` (or on the install screen).

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `watchFor` | `cost, security, data-loss, irreversible, customers, assumptions` | The topics to flag. A list; `all` means every topic, `none` turns checks off. Names that match no topic are ignored, and if none are left every topic is watched, so a typo never switches the reader off. |
| `maxChecksPerSession` | `30` | The spend cap: model checks allowed per session (0 to 1000). When it is reached, checks stop and the status line says so once. `0` turns checks off. |

## What it can touch

- **Model calls:** one completion on the `haiku` model per reply over 150 words, at low effort, with at most 1,024 output tokens and a 30 second time limit, and never more than `maxChecksPerSession` per session. It goes through your session's own client and provider. A failed call counts toward the cap. Nothing is spent in a run where nothing draws (`claude -p`).
- **What is sent:** the reply as written (whole up to 12,000 characters, beyond that its first 8,000 and last 4,000), including anything it quotes, and up to 40 lines naming this turn's tool calls and their targets: the first line of each command (up to 160 characters), a file or notebook path, a URL, a search pattern or query, a skill name, a subagent type, a tool call's description, and, for messaging tools, the recipient, the subject and the channel name (the `to`, `subject` and `channel` inputs). Nothing else from a tool's input. Before they are sent, secret-shaped strings in those commands and targets (bearer tokens, `PASSWORD=` or `api_key=` values, common API key formats, long hex or base64 strings) are replaced with `[hidden]`; this is best effort, and the reply itself is not masked. All of it is already in your conversation with the same provider. Never tool output, written file contents or edit text.
- **Reads:** the session transcript, through Claude Code, to find this turn's tool calls. No files, no processes, no network of its own.
- **Writes:** nothing on disk. Notes and the check count live in the session and end with it.
- **Explain more** starts one turn of your main model, at its normal cost, and only when you press it.
- `/fineprint` shows its list in a pane, not in the conversation, so the model never reads it. Where no surface can show a pane, the list is a transcript line, which the model does not read either.

## Limits

- A small model's judgment: it can miss things and can flag noise. It is a second reader, not a guarantee.
- Only main-conversation replies that finished normally are checked: not subagents, not interrupted or failed turns.
- "This turn's tool calls" are the calls since your last prompt. A row Claude Code adds that looks like a prompt can shorten that list.
- The band draws in the terminal and the desktop app. In other surfaces (VS Code, mobile) a note arrives as a toast instead, and `/fineprint` has the details.
- The note appears a few seconds after the turn ends, while the small model reads.
- If the model cannot be reached (for example, an organization policy blocks `haiku`), Fine Print shows one toast per session and otherwise stays quiet.
- The status line about the cap stays up for the rest of the session, unless you raise the cap or run `/clear`.
- `/clear` starts fresh: the notes, the band and the check count are reset with the conversation.
- Only the final message of a turn is read. A caveat in an earlier message of the same turn, followed by a short closing summary, is not seen.

# Footprints

A live file tree beside the chat that shows where Claude has been.

## Install

```
/plugin install footprints --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

- `/footprints` opens a pane with the project's file tree: docked beside the transcript in fullscreen, above the prompt otherwise. Because you asked, it opens at any terminal width, and it works while Claude is mid-turn. It adds nothing to the transcript (the model never reads it); the pane, or a toast, is the answer.
- As Claude works, names change color:
  - **blue** - read (Read, an @-mention; a folder Glob or Grep searched)
  - **amber** - edited; it shimmers while the edit is still running (only while the pane is on screen)
  - **green** - edited, then committed with `git commit`
  - **new** - created this session
  - ~~struck through~~ - deleted (a file created this session and then deleted leaves no trace)
  - **(shell)** - changed by a Bash command rather than an edit tool
- The header counts it up: `read 12 · edited 4 · new 1`, plus `deleted` and `committed` once there are any. New, deleted and committed files are counted in edited too.
- **Touched only**: press `t` while the pane has the keys (click it, or ctrl+x tab), or type `/footprints touched`. Every folder Claude did not touch collapses, and untouched files fold into one `+ N untouched files` line. A project with more than 50 folders opens this way, with a note under the header saying so; one press shows the whole tree, and your choice then stands for the session.
- **Status line**: `edited 4` under the prompt, so you see activity with the pane closed.
- Untouched folders with more than 40 files start collapsed, showing their file count. Files Claude touched outside the project are listed under `outside <folder>`.
- `/clear` starts a clean trail.

## Settings

None.

## What it can touch

- **Reads**: file names and modification times only, never contents. Names come from `git ls-files` (or a folder listing outside git). Around a Bash call it also reads the modification time of each file git reports as changed (up to 400, the ones the call moved first). It also reads the project folder's real path, and for a Glob or Grep target, whether it is a folder.
- **Runs** (all read-only, no index lock):
  - `git rev-parse --show-toplevel --show-prefix` to find the repo
  - `git ls-files -z --cached --others --exclude-standard -- . ':(exclude,glob)**/node_modules/**'` when you open the pane, and after a commit or checkout while it is open
  - `git --no-optional-locks status --porcelain=v2 ... -- ':/' ':(top,exclude,glob)**/node_modules/**'` before and after each Bash call, pane open or not (the "after" is skipped when the call was read-only). That is two runs per Bash call: tens of milliseconds in most repos, about 0.3 s together in a 100,000-file one. If one run takes over 2 seconds or times out, shell tracking pauses and the transcript says so once: `Footprints: shell tracking paused, git status is slow in this repo`. Read and edit tracking keep working, and running `/footprints` again turns shell tracking back on.
- **Writes**: nothing on disk; its marks live in the session's state.
- **Network**: none. **Model calls**: none.

## Limits

- In a repo where `git status` is slow (over 2 s), shell tracking pauses for the session.
- `node_modules` is always skipped, even where `.gitignore` does not list it, so files Claude reads or writes there show only when touched by an edit tool or Read.
- Shell changes need git. Outside a git repo the tree still works (a walk that skips `node_modules`, `.git` and a few cache folders, without `.gitignore`), but Bash changes are not marked.
- Shell attribution compares `git status` before and after the call plus file times, so: a branch switch that leaves git clean on both sides is not marked; a file you save in your own editor while a Bash command runs can be counted as changed by the shell; changes made by a background Bash command are not marked. With more than 400 files dirty, a file that was already dirty and is changed again may be missed.
- Green needs a Bash command that runs `git commit` and moves HEAD. Commits you make in your own terminal are not seen.
- Files read through the shell (`cat`, `rg`) do not turn blue; only Read, Glob, Grep and @-mentions count. Native macOS and Linux builds of Claude Code have no Glob or Grep tools, so folder marks mostly come from builds that do.
- `t` works only while the pane holds the keyboard; from the prompt, use `/footprints touched`.
- Subagents' tool calls count too.
- Big repos: it keeps up to 20,000 file names and draws up to 400 rows (the rest is one "more" line).
- An edit still running when the mod reloads is not recorded.
- A name holding control characters is drawn with color codes dropped and each other control character shown as `�` (git's file lists are read NUL-separated, so its path quoting never applies).
- Tested with POSIX paths (macOS, Linux). Colors follow your theme's `suggestion`, `warning` and `success`.

# Halftime

Claude works, you play. The whistle blows the moment it needs you.

Four small games live in the band above your prompt. The moment Claude needs
you - a permission prompt, a question, an input request, or the turn ending -
the game freezes, the board closes so your keys go back to the prompt, and a
line says `whistle: Claude needs you`. When Claude gets going again you get a
3-2-1 and the same run, exactly where you left it.

## Install

```
/plugin install halftime --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/halftime` | Opens the picker, with your one-line scorecard. |
| `/halftime cratehop` (or `tailchase`, `merge`, `sweep`) | Puts that game's daily board above the prompt. Add `practice` for a random board. |
| `/halftime auto` | Turns auto on or off (`/halftime auto on`, `/halftime auto off`). |
| `/halftime off` | Closes the band; a run in play is paused, and the picker offers it back. |

The command runs at once even while Claude is mid-turn. In the terminal and the
desktop app its replies are short toasts and nothing is added to the
conversation, so Claude never reads them. VS Code and the mobile app have no
band, so there the reply is the command's row: your one-line scorecard.

**A board takes your keys only when you click it.** No mouse (the classic
terminal renderer sends no clicks)? Press ctrl+x tab to focus the band, then
the letter keys drawn under the board (`w a s d`, `x f`, `p` to pause). Esc
hands the keys back to the prompt. No game ever uses Enter, `y`, `n` or a digit, and the board never
passes those keys on, so a stray press can never answer one of Claude Code's
prompts.

The games (all original):

- **cratehop** - a courier runs on its own; `space`, `up`, `w` or a click jumps the crates. The first ten seconds are gentle: a slow start (10 cells a second), a 4.5 second run-up to the first crate, low crates and wide gaps. Then it speeds up by about 0.18 cells a second every second, to a cap of 24 cells a second about a minute and a half in, and holds there. Every gap is a full jump plus a quarter second to react, every crate leaves a timing window of 250 ms or more, crates hurt a little less than they look (a graze is safe), and a jump pressed up to 120 ms before landing fires on touchdown. A crash bursts red where the courier was. Score: distance.
- **tailchase** - steer a snake on a wide, short field with the arrows, `wasd` or `hjkl`. The edges wrap; biting yourself ends the run. It starts slow (about 4 steps a second) and speeds up a little with every pip, to a cap of about 8 a second at 37 pips. A pip only ever lands on a cell your head can reach. Up to three turns wait in line for their step, and a step that would bite is held back for 100 ms, so a late turn still saves you. Score: pips eaten.
- **merge** - slide a 4x4 board of lettered tiers (arrows, `wasd`, `hjkl`); two equal letters make the next one, once per tile per move. It deals two A's in one line, so the first slide already makes a B; only A's are dealt for the first 12 moves, then an occasional B creeps in. A game can end, but never before move 14. Score: points.
- **sweep** - a 16x6 mine field with 12 mines. Arrows move, `space` or `x` opens, `f` flags, or click / right-click a cell. It opens with a safe pocket, and every board is checked by a solver before it is dealt: the single-cell rules plus the subset rule clear it from the opening, so you never have to guess. Score: seconds to clear (lower is better).

Every game's field is drawn centered between two dim rails, on a clear background: solid blocks for the snake, crates and tiles, raised slabs for sweep's closed cells. Every game: `p` pauses and resumes, `r` starts again after a run ends.

**Daily boards.** Each game's daily board comes from the date alone, so
everyone gets the same board that day. After a run, the result line reads like
`halftime daily 10-09 · cratehop 412 · played 3m of a 7m turn`, with a `copy` button.

**Auto mode** offers a game (a clickable line) once a turn has run 10 seconds.
It never starts a game or takes your keys by itself.

**The whistle** blows for: a permission prompt (from the main conversation or
a subagent), a question from Claude (AskUserQuestion), an input request from a
tool (MCP elicitation), and the main turn ending. Subagents starting and
finishing never pause or resume anything. The run comes back with a 3-2-1 when
the loop that asked moves on, or when your next turn starts; after a turn ends
you can also press `play on`.

The run also pauses by itself when a survey takes the band, when you start
typing at the prompt, when you open the picker or close the band, and when a
realtime game (cratehop, tailchase) gets no key or click for 20 seconds. A board
that comes back after any of these waits for your click.

## Settings

No settings screen. Auto mode (`/halftime auto`) and your last game are
remembered across sessions; the picker's `daily` / `practice` toggle lasts the
session.

## What it can touch

- **Its own store only** (Claude Code's per-plugin store): personal bests
  (`best:<game>`), today's daily best (`daily:<game>`), totals (play time,
  play time while Claude worked, runs), the auto switch and your last game.
- **The clipboard**, only when you press `copy`.
- **No files, no processes, no network, no model calls.**
- Timers run only while a game is played: the board's frame clock while a
  realtime run is in play and holds your keys, and a 3-second countdown. A
  paused or closed game ticks and redraws nothing. Auto mode sets one 10-second
  timer per turn.

## Limits

- In the desktop app, a `/halftime` sent as the very first prompt of a new session may show "/halftime isn't a command here." The app checks the command before mods have registered theirs; the command still runs, and later ones show no such line.
- **Terminal and desktop app only.** VS Code and the mobile app have no band
  and no board; there `/halftime` shows a one-line scorecard instead.
- **Starting a game cannot hand it your keys.** Claude Code gives the band the
  keyboard only on your click or its focus chord (ctrl+x tab), so
  `/halftime cratehop` puts the board up and the run starts on your first
  click or key.
- **Esc gives no signal to the mod.** A realtime run you leave keeps going
  until you type at the prompt (it pauses then) or, at most, 20 seconds with
  no key or click, when it pauses itself. Those idle seconds never count as
  play. Turn-based games (merge, sweep) never tick, so they need no such pause.
- **After you answer a permission prompt**, play resumes when that step's tools
  finish (the API has no "dialog answered" event), or at your next turn.
- **Two open sessions** share bests safely (each save re-reads the store just
  before writing and repairs a lower write it finds after), but the store has no
  true compare-and-set: two saves in the same instant can still race. Totals are
  added the same way and can, rarely, miss a few seconds.
- Copy works in the terminal; a surface without a clipboard path says so, and
  the line stays on screen to select.
- The daily board follows your machine's calendar day.
- cratehop's top speed leaves a quarter second to see and answer a crate on a band at least 24 columns wide; on a narrower one the courier sees too little of the course to be fair at the cap.
- Drawing is verified against the plugin test kit, not a real terminal's paint.

# Hatchling

A collectible pixel pet that hatches, reacts and evolves while you code.

## Install

```
/plugin install hatchling --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

An egg appears in a small band above your prompt: Bolt's egg, in the modmyclaude mascot's lime with
its antenna light on. It wobbles while Claude works, cracks a little more at a quarter, half and three
quarters of the way, and hatches after 25 tool calls into one of 8 original species, or something rarer:

| Species | Rarity | Odds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pebblet (a mossy river stone), Fluffle (lop-eared fluff), Coilsnail (snail with a thread-spool shell) | common | 36 in 64 (56%) |
| Nimbit (a pocket raincloud), Lampwing (a moth with a glowing belly) | uncommon | 18 in 64 (28%) |
| Foldling (a folded paper bird), Geobug (a beetle with a geode shell) | rare | 8 in 64 (12.5%) |
| Starwhelp (a teacup-sized star dragon) | legendary | 2 in 64 (3%) |
| ??? | secret | 1 in 100 |

The species odds apply to the other 99 eggs in 100. Each species has a 1 in 64 chance to be shiny
(another palette). The roll happens once, at hatch time, and is saved: restarting never rerolls. The
egg carries its own random seed, so two sessions that hatch it at the same moment hatch the same pet.

What it does while you work:

- **Bounces** when a tool call succeeds, **sweats** when one fails, **cheers** when a Bash command
  prints a passing test run (jest, vitest, pytest, go test, cargo test and nextest, node:test, mocha,
  rspec, bun, deno, phpunit, unittest, dotnet test, Playwright).
- **Falls asleep** after 5 minutes with nothing happening, and wakes on the next prompt or tool call.
- **Grows**: 1 XP per tool call (including those Claude's subagents make), 5 per finished turn of
  your own, 5 more for a passing test run. It becomes a teen at 200 XP and an adult at 800 XP, each
  with a short celebration and a toast.

Commands:

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/pet` | Stat card: name, species, rarity, shiny or not, stage, XP to the next stage, days together |
| `/pet name <name>` | Rename it (up to 16 letters, numbers, spaces, `-` `'` `.` `_`). Works on the egg too. Answers with a toast. |
| `/pet hide` / `/pet show` | Hide or bring back the band (remembered across sessions). Answers with a toast. |
| `/pet card` | A ~30 x 12 plain-text card with a **Copy card** button, for sharing |

The pet is one pet for you, across every session and project. It shares the band with other mods:
theirs is drawn first and the pet below it, so it never pushes their buttons out of view.

## Settings

None.

## What it can touch

- **Files**: none directly. The pet is saved in the mod's own store (a JSON file Claude Code keeps
  for each plugin under your config directory).
- **Processes, network, model calls**: none. Everything is deterministic except the one hatch roll,
  which uses the platform's crypto random source.
- **What the model sees**: the text of `/pet` and `/pet card` (a few short lines), like any command's
  output. `/pet name`, `hide`, `show` and help answer with a toast the model never reads. Tool calls
  are only observed, never changed or refused.
- **Clipboard**: only when you press Copy card.

## Limits

- The band draws in the terminal and the desktop app's Code tab. VS Code and mobile have no band
  above the prompt; `/pet` and `/pet card` still work there as text.
- The desktop app draws the sprite as text cells too. How crisp it looks depends on the app's font and
  line spacing: generous line spacing can show thin seams between rows of pixels.
- "Tests passed" is read from the runner's summary in the Bash output. A runner with an unusual
  summary is not recognised (no cheer, no harm). Commands that only show a log (`cat`, `grep`,
  `gh run view`, `docker logs`, `kubectl logs`, also after a `cd` or wrapped in `sudo`, `env`, a
  subshell or `bash -c`) do not count. Test runs started in
  the background, very long outputs whose summary is cut, and PowerShell are not read.
- Animation runs on a timer only while something happens (a reaction, Claude working, the doze-off);
  when idle, asleep or hidden no timer runs.
- Two sessions open at once share the one pet. Each change re-reads the saved pet first, so progress
  from both sessions adds up, and a pet that has hatched is never rolled again. Two writes in the same
  instant can still lose one tool call's XP. Another session's progress shows in this band at this
  session's next event.
- When hidden, the pet still counts tool calls and turns, and still toasts when it hatches or evolves.

# Headway

See how far along Claude is, and when it will land.

```
Build · Wire the routes (2/6) ▰▰▱▱▱▱ ~3m left
```

## Install

```
/plugin install headway --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

Nothing to set up. Headway reads the plan Claude already keeps and draws one line above your prompt while that plan is in progress:

- **Where the plan comes from:** Claude's own todo list (TodoWrite), its task tools (TaskCreate, TaskUpdate, TaskList) and the plan you approve in plan mode (ExitPlanMode). Plan-mode headings become stages; a flat todo list is one stage. A todo list that follows an approved plan is placed into the plan's stages by matching step titles.
- **The line:** stage, current step, steps done out of total, a bar, and time left.
- **Time left** appears once two steps have finished. It is the median time per step this session, blended with this project's pace from earlier sessions, times the steps left. When step times vary too much to be honest it says `estimating...` instead.
- **Running long:** a step past three times its estimate turns amber and says how long it has run (`7m 12s on this step`).
- **Plans that change:** when Claude rewrites its list, reworded steps that were done stay done, and the line flashes `plan revised +2 −1` for a few seconds.
- **Done:** the bar turns green for a few seconds, then a toast gives the receipt (`Plan done in 4m 12s, 18s ahead of estimate. Build 2m 1s · Verify 2m 11s`) and the line leaves.
- **Subagents:** while any run, a small `3 agents` chip sits at the end of the line. No agent details.
- **Other mods:** Headway adds its line beneath what other mods draw above the prompt and passes theirs through, so when the band runs out of rows it is Headway's line that gets cut, never another mod's buttons. A mod that takes the whole band hides Headway's line until that mod is done. Headway steps aside while a survey holds that space.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/headway` | Opens a pane with every step, its status (`[x]` done, `[>]` current, `[ ]` to do) and its time, plus a button to hide or show the line. Works mid-turn. |
| `/headway hide` | Hides the line for this session. |
| `/headway show` | Shows it again. |

### For other mods: the "plan done" moment

Each time a plan finishes, Headway writes the `$.state` value `headway.done`: `{ seq, at, totalMs, steps, stageMs, estimateMs }` (counts and durations, never titles). Its type is in [`types/index.d.ts`](types/index.d.ts) as `HeadwayDone`; list `headway` under `dependencies` in your `plugin.json` to get it typed. Then either:

- read it while drawing, `await $.state.get({ plugin: 'headway', key: 'done' })`, and your render hook redraws whenever a plan finishes, or
- react the moment it is written:

```ts
on('state.set', { plugin: 'headway', key: 'done' }, async ($, e, next) => {
  if (e.value) $.ui.toast(`${e.value.steps} steps done`)
  return next(e)
})
```

## Settings

None.

## What it can touch

- **Files:** none directly. Per-project pace history goes in the mod's own store (`$.store`, a JSON file Claude Code keeps for the mod): step durations, plan counts and when each project was last updated (to keep the most recent), never step titles. Projects are keyed by a hash of the project root, not the path. Capped at the last 40 step times for each of the 30 most recent projects.
- **Processes, network, model calls:** none. No tokens where Claude Code has its own plan tools: it adds nothing to the prompt or the system prompt. Where Headway lends its plan tool, that tool's short description sits in Claude's tool list, and Claude's calls to it cost what a todo update does. It never refuses a tool call and never holds up the end of a turn. `/headway` answers with no text for the model; the pane and toasts never reach it.
- **Timer:** one, once a second, only while a plan is in progress and Claude (or a subagent) is working, on a surface that draws the band (the terminal or the desktop app). It also runs for the moment a finished plan's green bar shows (3 seconds) or "plan revised" shows (4 seconds), even while Claude is idle. It stops when Claude is idle, when you hide the line, when the plan is done and when nothing draws the band.
- **Sounds:** none.

## Limits

- In the desktop app, a `/headway` sent as the very first prompt of a new session may show "/headway isn't a command here." The app checks the command before mods have registered theirs; the command still runs, and later ones show no such line.
- Time counts only while Claude or a subagent is working, so a pause between turns never makes a step look slow. A step's time is the span since the previous step finished; steps finished together share it.
- Time left hides (`estimating...`) while the sample coefficient of variation of the last 8 step times is above 1.0, roughly when one step took six times another. One long step (a full test run among quick edits) stops hiding it once eight newer steps have finished; the per-step median still uses the whole session.
- A plan-mode plan with no todo or task list after it has no progress to read. Headway shows `Plan approved · 2 stages, 6 steps` until that turn ends, then clears it.
- A plan Claude stops updating (you interrupted, changed topic, or the last items were never marked done) leaves on its own once two of Claude's turns pass with no update to it: no receipt and no history for it. An approved plan-mode outline no list followed expires the same way. A `/clear` or resuming another conversation clears the plan at once.
- Plan-mode parsing is a heuristic: the shallowest heading level used at least twice is the stage level, top-level list items are steps, and sections such as Context, Risks or Files to change are left out.
- Matching a reworded step is fuzzy (letter-pair overlap of 75% or word overlap of 60%). Very different wording reads as one step removed and one added. A done step keeps its done only while the new wording keeps 60% of its words, so a sibling such as "Write tests for the UI" never inherits the done of "Write tests for the API".
- Todo lists and plans kept by subagents are not shown; only the main conversation's plan is. Task updates from subagents do count for tasks Headway already knows.
- The agents chip counts subagents from start to finish. Teammates are left out, since they idle between turns.
- The "plan done" signal is a `$.state` value, not a telemetry mark: marks feed Claude Code's own analytics, which a display-only mod should not touch.
- After a plugin reload the countdown resumes at Claude's next tool call or turn.
- Drawn on the terminal and the desktop app, the two surfaces with a band above the prompt. The `/headway` pane opens on any surface that places panes.
- Where Claude has no todo or task tool (the desktop app, and terminal builds without todo tools), Headway lends it a small plan tool, `plan`, shaped like TodoWrite and listed with Claude's other tools, so the line still follows Claude's plan. Claude decides whether to use it: a turn where it plans only in prose shows nothing. Where Claude Code has its own plan tools, Headway lends none.
- Titles are drawn without escape sequences, control characters or invisible marks (bidi overrides, zero-width characters), and the line is laid out in terminal cells, so wide (CJK) titles and emoji are cut to fit rather than wrapping.

Build me a Claude Code mod called "last-look" that holds destructive commands until I approve them and shows what they would destroy.

What it catches (Bash tool calls)
- rm -r / rm -rf, find ... -delete, git clean -fd(x), git reset --hard, git checkout -- . and git restore ., git push --force (even with --force-with-lease alongside), git branch -D, git worktree remove --force, and redirects that overwrite an existing file (> file). Parse `--` (end of options) in every git rule.

What it shows
- A side pane (a band above the prompt on narrow terminals) with the command, what it would affect (each file to be deleted and the total size, or the commits or branch to be lost) and two buttons, Proceed and Cancel. Cancel is the default and Enter cancels. Proceed has no hotkey and the pane never takes the keyboard, so nothing I type can approve a command. While a hold is pending, draw it alone.

What is new here
- Git-aware: highlight files with uncommitted changes, because git cannot bring those back ("3 files have unsaved work you would lose").
- Handles compound commands such as cd some/path && rm -rf build by measuring relative to the cd target.
- An alwaysAllow setting for paths that are fine to delete without asking, e.g. dist, build, .next, coverage: only for rm with plain literal paths whose real path is inside an allowed folder, never for find or anything that follows links.
- The classifier decides whether to hold; measuring only fills in the details. If it cannot measure a command (globs, braces, variables, odd find options), it still holds it and says "could not measure: review it yourself". Skip a hold only on positive proof covering the whole command (e.g. a single redirect to a plain path that does not exist yet).

Guardrails
- A safety net, not a permission system: say so in the pane footer. Measure with read-only commands only (ls, du, find without -delete or any write or exec option, git status, git log). Strip control characters from anything drawn.
- If the mod itself errors, deny the command instead of letting it run.

Build rules
- Mods are new (Claude Code 2.1.287+). Use your plugin-authoring skill and read the types it points to before writing anything.
- Only do what is described here: no network calls and no reading files the mod does not need, unless this prompt says so.
- Write at least one test for the main behaviour and run `claude plugin validate` and `claude plugin test` until both pass.

- When I say it is good, install it so it loads in every session, and tell me where it lives and how to turn it off.
