# Last Look

Holds destructive commands until you approve, and shows what they would destroy.

## Install

```
/plugin install last-look --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

There is nothing to run. When a shell command Claude is about to run (through the Bash tool, or the Monitor tool's command) is one of the destructive kinds below, Last Look holds it before it runs, measures what it would destroy, and asks you. Once a command is recognised as destructive it is **always** held: measuring only adds detail to the hold and never lets a command through.

- **Where it asks.** A pane when the terminal has room for one (Claude Code places a pane nobody asked for from 144 columns: docked beside the transcript in fullscreen, inline above the prompt otherwise). On narrower terminals, a band directly above the prompt. The desktop app works the same way.
- **What it shows.** The command, and for each destructive part of it: every file it would delete with the total size (cut to the room there is, then "and N more"), files with unsaved work highlighted first ("3 files have unsaved work you would lose"), and the commits or branch that would be lost. When its measurement comes back empty or fails, the hold says so ("Nothing found at these paths" for plain paths, otherwise "could not measure: review it yourself"); either way you decide.
- **Deciding.** Keys you type never approve: the pane and the band never take the keyboard on their own, and Proceed has no hotkey. Click a button, or press ctrl+x tab to move into the pane or band; Cancel then has the focus, so Enter (or `c`) cancels. Proceed takes a click, or Tab onto it and then Enter. In the pane, Esc closes it and cancels. While a command is held in the band, the band shows only the hold (other mods' bands are hidden until you decide), so nothing another mod draws can hide its buttons.
- **After.** Cancel tells Claude the command did not run and not to work around it. Proceed lets the command go on to Claude Code's usual permission check and run. A dim line in the transcript records each decision, and the status line says when a command is waiting.

Compound commands are understood: `cd web && rm -rf build` is measured inside `web`, and so are subshells, `bash -c '...'`, `$(...)`, `sudo`, `env`, quoted paths, `~`, `$HOME`, globs and `{a,b}` / `{1..9}` braces.

### What it holds

| Command | Measured with |
| --- | --- |
| `rm -r`, `rm -rf`, `rm -fr`, `rm --recursive` (any flag order) | the files and total size, git status of each |
| `find ... -delete`, `find ... -exec rm` (also `-exec sudo rm`, `-exec sh -c ...`) | the same `find` re-run as a listing (`-delete` becomes `-print0`); never re-run when it holds `-fprint`, `-fls`, another `-exec`, or a test the system find reads differently (`-regex`, `-readable`) |
| `... \| xargs rm` | held as "could not measure" (its targets come from the previous command) |
| `git clean -f`, `-fd`, `-fdx`, `-ffdx` | `git clean -n` with the same flags, `-f -f` included (so nested repositories show), as a dry run |
| `git reset --hard [ref]` | uncommitted changes discarded, commits dropped from the branch |
| `git checkout -- <paths>`, `git checkout .`, `git checkout <file>`, `git checkout -f`, `git restore <paths>`, `git switch --discard-changes` | uncommitted changes in those paths |
| `git push --force`, `-f`, `+refspec`, `--mirror`, even beside `--force-with-lease` (a lease alone is not held) | commits on the remote branch that yours lacks, as of your last fetch |
| `git branch -D`, `git branch --delete --force` (`--` before the names too) | commits that exist only on that branch |
| `git worktree remove --force` / `-f` | held as "could not measure": it deletes the worktree folder and any uncommitted work in it |
| `> file`, `2> file`, `&> file`, `>\| file` onto an existing file (not `>>`, not `/dev/null`) | the file's size and git status |

Every one of these is held even when nothing is found to destroy (`rm -rf build` with no `build`, `git reset --hard` on a clean tree): the hold says what it found. Only two cases run untouched, and only on positive proof that they destroy nothing:
- a redirect (`> new.txt`) when the whole command is that one simple command (no `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, `&`, newline, subshell, `$(...)` or unquoted here-doc: an earlier part could create the file first), its target is a plain literal path (no `$VAR`, `~`, glob, braces, `..`, `$(...)` or backticks), and the file system answers that it **does not exist**. Any other answer (a permission error, a link, a folder, a path it cannot read) holds;
- a bare `git checkout <name>` (no `-f`, `--force`, `--`, extra paths or other options; `<name>` a plain token) when git confirms `<name>` is a local branch, a remote-tracking branch, or the one remote branch it would set up, and no file of that name makes it ambiguous. A git error, a tag or commit, or any doubt holds. (git itself refuses a branch switch that would lose changes.)

## Settings

Every setting has a default, so the notice at install about options not yet set is expected; change them in `/config`.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `alwaysAllow` | `dist,build,.next,coverage,node_modules/.cache` | Folders that are fine to delete with `rm -r` without asking. It never covers `find` (with `-L`, `-H` or `-follow` it reaches through links), redirects or git. A relative entry matches that run of folder names anywhere beneath the project root (`dist` matches `packages/web/dist`, not `distro`, and never the root itself); an absolute entry matches by prefix. A command passes only when **every** path it touches is a plain literal path (no glob, braces, `$VAR`, `~`, `..` or `$(...)`) that exists, and both its spelling and where its links lead are inside an allowed folder. Leave it empty to hold everything. |

## What it can touch

- **Reads:** file metadata only (stat, and directory listings to expand globs) for the paths a destructive command names. Never file contents.
- **Runs** (by argv, no shell, read-only): the system `find` (never with `-delete`, `-exec`, `-ok`, `-fprint`, `-fprint0`, `-fprintf` or `-fls`), `du -sk`, and `git rev-parse`, `status`, `ls-files`, `for-each-ref` (to tell a branch name from a path on a bare `git checkout <name>`), `diff-index --numstat`, `diff-files --numstat`, `rev-list`, `log` and `clean -n` (a dry run). Git runs with `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0` and fsmonitor off, and plain `git diff` (which rewrites the index) is never used, so git writes nothing. To count changed lines git reads the changed files' contents. While a command is held it keeps one `sleep 1` running at a time (PowerShell `Start-Sleep` on Windows): Claude Code pauses a hook's time limit only while a host call is in flight.
- **Environment:** reads `HOME`.
- **Network:** none. Git never fetches, so force-push numbers are as of your last fetch.
- **Model calls:** none.
- **Writes:** nothing outside its own session state.

## Limits

- A safety net, not a permission system. It reads the command's text, so it does not see:
  - commands inside scripts or piped into a shell (`./clean.sh`, `npm run clean`, `make clean`, `echo ... | bash`, `bash <<EOF`, `bash script.sh`);
  - a program named only at run time (`$(echo rm) -rf`, `"$RM" -rf`, `eval $CMD`), shell and git aliases, flags hidden in variables (`rm $FLAGS dir`);
  - other interpreters and tools (`python -c`, `node -e`, `perl -e`, `rsync --delete`, `grm`, `busybox rm`, `parallel rm`, `ssh host rm`, `docker run ... rm`);
  - other ways to destroy files or history (`mv` or `cp` over a file, `sed -i`, `tee`, `truncate`, `dd`, `git stash drop`/`clear`, `git push --delete` or `origin :branch`, `git checkout -B`, `git switch -C`, `git rm -r`, `git reset --merge`, `git gc --prune`, database commands).
- `rm` without `-r` (any number of plain files, `rm *` included) is left alone on purpose, and so are the other one-file-at-a-time tools treated like it: `shred`, `unlink`, `ln -sf` over a file.
- Only the Bash tool and the Monitor tool's command are held. The Edit and Write tools are not.
- It measures with the system `find`; the shell's own `find` (Claude Code's bundled one, or GNU find) can match a little differently, so a listing is a guide, and an empty or failed one holds as "could not measure".
- zsh's `**` patterns, and brace expressions past 256 words, are held as "could not measure" rather than guessed at.
- Proceed does not skip Claude Code's own permission prompt: in the default mode you may be asked again.
- Force-push measurements use your remote-tracking branches, which may be out of date.
- Sizes are disk usage from `du`. Up to 8 destructive parts of one command are measured; any past that are held as unmeasured. Each `find` or `du` gets 8 seconds.
- Your home folder, `/` and top-level system folders are never walked: they are held with a plain warning instead.
- With nobody to ask (a `claude -p` run) a destructive command is denied. In a session drawn only on mobile or VS Code where the pane cannot be placed, it is denied too, and the reason says so.
- The band gives way while a Claude Code survey holds it; the pane does not.
- macOS and Linux. On Windows, `find` and `du` are usually missing, so commands are held as "could not measure".
- A held command waits as long as you do. Interrupting the turn (Esc at the prompt) stops it.
- Two paths are verified by reading the code, not by tests (the test kit cannot raise them): closing the pane by hand or Esc counts as Cancel, and interrupting the turn denies the held command.
- With several holds queued, if you move the focus onto Proceed (Tab) and press Enter, the next hold may draw with the focus still on its Proceed: read each hold before pressing Enter again. Not verified live.

# Noted

Turns your corrections into permanent rules, without duplicates.

## Install

```
/plugin install noted --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

Correct Claude the way you normally would: "no, use pnpm", "don't add comments to every line", "we use vitest, not jest", "stop adding emojis", "I told you to use tabs". Your prompt goes through untouched. A moment later a band appears above the prompt with one short, general rule:

```
Noted - save this as a house rule?
Use pnpm, not npm, in this repo.
[ Save to project ] [ Save globally ] [ Edit ] [ Skip ]
```

- **Save to project** appends it to `./CLAUDE.md`, **Save globally** to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, as a list item under a `## House rules` heading (added if missing). Nothing else in the file changes.
- **Edit** turns the rule into a text field. Press Enter to keep your wording, then save.
- **Skip** drops it.
- If the rule is already there (same words, or the same meaning), the band says **already a rule** instead of proposing it again.
- If it contradicts a rule you already have, the band shows the old rule and offers **Replace old rule**, which rewrites that line in place, instead of adding a contradiction.

Once the band has focus (click it, or ctrl+x tab), `e` edits, `s` skips, `o` dismisses a notice and `d` closes the `/rules` list. The buttons that write a file (Save, Replace old rule, Remove) have no key, and focus starts on Skip, OK or Done, so neither a stray keystroke nor Enter ever writes one. noted's lines come after any other mod's band, never in place of it, so their buttons stay in view.

`/rules` lists the rules noted has learned, with the file and the date each was added, in the transcript and in the band, where each one has a **Remove** button. `/rules remove <number>` removes one by its number, for surfaces without the band; it acts only when you type it, and a peer session, channel, task or plugin running it gets a refusal. Removing a rule deletes its line from the file. The `/rules` listing is a transcript row, so Claude reads it too.

## Settings

None.

## What it can touch

- **Files read:** `./CLAUDE.md` at the project root and `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (or `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/CLAUDE.md` when that is set), only to find the `## House rules` list. They are read when a correction is detected, when you press a button and when you run `/rules`.
- **Files written:** those two files and nothing else, and only after you press Save, Replace old rule or Remove, or run `/rules remove <number>`. A file that exists but cannot be read is never written.
- **Environment:** `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `USERPROFILE` and `HOME` (in that order), to find the global file.
- **Transcript:** the last 600 characters of Claude's previous reply, as context for the rule.
- **Model calls:** one per prompt that passes a keyword pre-filter, never for other prompts. It uses the `haiku` alias at low effort and sends the correction (up to 600 characters), that reply tail, and up to 60 existing rules (200 characters each). That is at most about 4,000 input tokens and usually a few hundred. The existing rules, like the correction and the reply tail, are sent as quoted data the model is told not to follow, and nothing is written until you press a button. The reply is capped at 1,024 tokens, room for the model to think first, and the call at 20 seconds. A reply cut short is ignored. The call goes through the session's own client.
- **Store:** noted's own store keeps each saved rule's text, file and date, so `/rules` can show when it was added.
- **Network and processes:** none of its own.

## Limits

- The pre-filter matches English phrasing. Corrections in other languages, and prompts over 800 characters, are not picked up.
- Only prompts you type (terminal, Remote Control, desktop app) are read. Prompts from tools, plugins, peers and schedules are ignored.
- The band draws in the terminal and the desktop app. In VS Code or on mobile, noted says once that corrections there are not captured. `/rules` works everywhere.
- The model call runs after your prompt has entered, alongside Claude's reply, so it never slows the turn. If you interrupt the turn while it runs, that suggestion may be lost.
- If the session cannot use the `haiku` model (some Bedrock, Vertex or gateway setups, refused or answered as "model not found"), noted says so once and proposes nothing.
- "Same meaning" duplicates and conflicts are judged by the model, which sees the first 60 existing rules. Same-words duplicates are caught in every rule, without the model.
- `/rules` lists only rules saved through noted. Rules you write by hand still count for duplicates and conflicts. A rule you delete by hand drops off the list.
- Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md when a session starts, so a saved rule steers Claude from the next session on. The correction you just typed is already in the current conversation.
- A CLAUDE.md that is not valid UTF-8 text is left alone, and so is one where a code fence that never closes would swallow the new rule. Line endings are kept. Removing the last rule leaves the heading in place.
- Terminal escapes and control characters are stripped from a rule before it is written, and shown as a placeholder in the band when they sit in rules you already have; those lines in your file are never touched.

## Built from a prompt

This mod was built from [`prompts/noted.md`](../../prompts/noted.md).

# Pager

Plays a sound when Claude finishes, needs you or hits an error.

Look away while Claude works. Pager plays one short sound, with a toast naming the session, when:

- **done** - a turn finished and it ran at least `minDuration` seconds (quick back-and-forth stays quiet),
- **needs you** - Claude is waiting on a permission prompt, a question, a plan approval or an MCP input request,
- **error** - a turn ended on an API error or a refusal.

## Install

```
/plugin install pager --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/pager` | Shows the pack, whether sounds are on, and your settings. |
| `/pager pack <classic\|arcade\|zen\|butler\|coach>` | Switches the sound pack. `/pager pack` alone lists them. |
| `/pager test` | Plays all three sounds of the current pack, one after another (even while muted). |
| `/pager mute <duration>` | Silences sounds and phone pushes for `30m`, `2h`, `1h 30m`, `45s` or `1d` (up to 7 days; a bare number is minutes; no duration means 1 hour). |
| `/pager unmute` | Ends a mute early. |

`/pager` runs at once, even while a turn is running, so you can mute mid-turn. Its answers show as a toast and stay out of the conversation, so Claude never reads them and they cost no tokens. Only you can change Pager: a `/pager` run that comes from a peer session, a channel relay, a background task or another plugin can read the status but cannot mute, unmute, switch packs or play the test (typed at the terminal, in the desktop app or through Remote Control all count as you).

Session titles and folder names are cleaned before a toast shows them: terminal escape codes are removed and other control characters become a replacement mark.

The five packs, all made for this mod. Three are synthesized tones:

- **classic** - soft bell tones
- **arcade** - 8-bit blips
- **zen** - gentle chimes

Two are spoken, one short original line per event in a generated voice (no game lines, no imitation of anyone), under a second and a half each, at the same loudness as the tones:

- **butler** - dry and formal: "Done." / "It needs you." / "Something went wrong."
- **coach** - upbeat: "That one's done." / "Your turn." / "We hit a snag."

Guardrails: one sound per event at most, and never more than one sound every 5 seconds in a session. Alerts inside that gap, while muted, or in quiet hours still show their toast; only the sound and the phone push are skipped.

## Settings

Every setting has a default, so the notice at install about options not yet set is expected. Set them in `/config` (or when you enable the plugin).

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `minDuration` | `20` | Seconds a turn must run before its done sound plays. Errors and needs-you always page. |
| `quietHours` | empty (off) | A local time window with no sound or push, such as `22:00-07:00`. It may wrap midnight. |
| `ntfyTopic` | empty (off) | An [ntfy.sh](https://ntfy.sh) topic for phone pushes. Stored as a secret. A pasted `https://ntfy.sh/<topic>` works too. |

The pack and a mute are kept in the plugin's store, so they last across sessions and apply to every session at once.

## What it can touch

- **Sound:** plays its own nine WAV files from `sounds/` through Claude Code's audio player.
- **Files:** reads and writes none of your files. The pack and mute end time live in the plugin's own store, a small JSON file Claude Code keeps for it in your Claude Code configuration folder.
- **Processes:** none of its own (Claude Code runs `afplay` to play a clip on macOS).
- **Network:** only when you set `ntfyTopic`. Each alert that makes a sound also sends one HTTPS POST to `https://ntfy.sh/<topic>` with a fixed title (`Pager: done`, `Pager: needs you`, `Pager: error`) and a short fixed text (for done, the turn's length, such as "A turn finished after 2m 5s."). It never sends your prompts, Claude's answers, the session title or the project name. This is the only network call Pager makes. Anyone who knows an ntfy.sh topic can read it, so pick a long, unguessable one.
- **Model calls:** none.

## How "needs you" is detected

Pager listens for Claude Code's own Notification event and pages on the types that mean a dialog is waiting on you: `permission_prompt`, `worker_permission_prompt`, `elicitation_dialog`, `elicitation_url_dialog` and `agent_needs_input`. Claude Code raises these once a dialog has waited about 6 seconds without a keypress, so a prompt you answer right away makes no sound. `idle_prompt` is left out because it follows a finished turn: a long one already paged, and a short one means you were there.

## Limits

- **Sound plays on macOS only.** Claude Code plays clips with `afplay`; on Linux and Windows it has no player, so `$.audio.play` is silent there. Toasts and phone pushes still work. `/pager test` says so.
- An interrupted turn (Esc, or a plugin cutting the turn for you) makes no sound: you were there.
- Pager stays silent (no sound, push or toast) when nothing draws the session: a plain `claude -p` run, or a desktop session with no window attached.
- Each session keeps its own 5 second gap, so two sessions ending together can both sound.
- If `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_PERMISSION_PROMPT_NOTIFY_HOOKS` is set, Claude Code raises no permission notification in the desktop app or SDK, so needs-you stays silent there.
- Subagent turns never page on their own; the main turn that ran them does.
- `minDuration` counts the whole turn, including time a permission prompt waited on you.
- Quiet hours use the clock of the machine running Claude Code.
- A hot reload of the plugin forgets the 5 second gap and the session title until the next prompt (at most one early sound, or a toast showing the folder name). A /clear forgets the title on purpose, so the old conversation's name does not linger.
- If ntfy.sh is down or offline, the push is dropped (noted in the debug log); the sound still plays.

## The sounds are original

Every clip is computed from sine and pulse waves by [`tools/synth.py`](tools/synth.py), using only the Python standard library. Regenerate them, byte for byte, with:

```
python3 -I mods/pager/tools/synth.py
```

Build me a Claude Code mod called "play-by-play" that replays every change Claude made in a turn, one step at a time.

What it does
- After a turn that changed files, show a hint above my prompt: "4 edits · 3 files · +38 −12 · press r or /replay".

What is new here
- Shell changes too: snapshot git diff before and after each Bash call, so renames and edits made by commands appear as steps, marked "via shell".
- A scoreboard at the top: files touched, lines added and removed, and the biggest change.
- /replay <n> replays an earlier turn (keep the last 10 turns of the session).
- A jump list: press a number to jump to a file's first change.

Guardrails
- Read-only: it never reverts or edits anything. Deterministic, no model calls.

Build rules
- Mods are new (Claude Code 2.1.287+). Use your plugin-authoring skill and read the types it points to before writing anything.
- Only do what is described here: no network calls and no reading files the mod does not need, unless this prompt says so.
- Write at least one test for the main behaviour and run `claude plugin validate` and `claude plugin test` until both pass.
- Load it in this session so I can try it, then take my changes in plain words.
- When I say it is good, install it so it loads in every session, and tell me where it lives and how to turn it off.

# Play-by-Play

Replays every change Claude made in a turn, shell edits included.

## Install

```
/plugin install play-by-play --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

- After a turn that changed files, a hint shows above the prompt:
  `4 edits · 3 files · +38 −12 · press r or /replay`, with a **Replay** and a **Hide** button.
  `r` and `x` press them once the band has the keyboard (click it, or ctrl+x tab).
- `/replay` opens a pane on the latest turn. `/replay <n>` opens an earlier one: 1 is the latest,
  up to 10 turns that changed files are kept. It runs at once, even while Claude is working, and shows
  only finished turns: a turn still running is never shown half done (the pane says one is in progress),
  and an open pane stays on its turn when the running one ends. The command answers the model nothing;
  its messages are toasts. A headless run, with no pane, gets the steps as text.
- The pane shows, top to bottom:
  - a scoreboard: files touched, lines added and removed, edit count, and the file with the biggest change;
  - a jump list of the files, numbered 1-9 in the order they were first changed;
  - **Prev**, **Next** and **Close**, and "Step 2 of 5";
  - the step: file name, what happened (edit, write, create, delete, rename, cell), `+/−` counts,
    **via shell** when a command made it, and the diff with removed lines red and added lines green.
    A binary file shows as "binary file changed (N bytes)", never as a diff.
- Keys while the pane has the keyboard (it takes it when `/replay` opens it):

  | Key | Does |
  | --- | --- |
  | `n` | next step |
  | `p` | previous step |
  | `1`-`9` | first change of that file |
  | `q`, Esc | close |
  | arrow keys | after a click on the pane's "Keys" line: left/up previous, right/down next |
  | up / down | without that click, only on a step taller than the pane |

  The mouse wheel and Page Up / Page Down still scroll a long diff.

## Settings

None.

## What it can touch

- **Reads**: the records the Edit, Write and NotebookEdit tools return (the text before and after), and
  the first 80 characters of each prompt you send, kept in the session's memory for the turn's header in
  the pane. It never opens a file itself.
- **Runs**: around every Bash command, read-only or not, read-only git plumbing in the session's folder,
  each with `--no-optional-locks`: `git rev-parse`, `git diff-index -p`, `git ls-files --others`,
  `git hash-object` (without `-w`), and for changed files `git show <HEAD>:<path>`,
  `git cat-file --batch-check` and `git diff --no-index` (an untracked file). Porcelain `git diff` is not used,
  because it rewrites `.git/index`. Nothing is staged, stashed, committed or written, and `.git/index` is
  never touched.
- **Cost**: 3 or 4 git calls before each command and 2 or 3 after it (none after one Claude Code marks
  read-only, such as `ls`), plus one or two per changed file. Each diffs the whole uncommitted tree against
  HEAD, and `hash-object` reads every untracked, unignored file, up to 500 of them (past that, untracked
  files are listed by name and their contents are not read). In a 100,000-file repository that is about
  half a second per command, and slower after many files were touched (a checkout, a formatter) until
  your own `git status` refreshes the index; see the pause below.
- **Writes**: nothing. It never reverts or edits a file. What it records lives in the session's memory
  and is gone when the session ends.
- **Network**: none. **Model calls**: none.

## Limits

- Shell changes need a git repository at the session's folder. Elsewhere commands run unwatched.
- Files git ignores (`node_modules`, build output) are not tracked, by design.
- An untracked file a command changes or deletes shows as a step without lines, since git kept no
  earlier copy, unless a file tool wrote that file earlier in the session.
- A file you save in your editor while a command waits for approval or runs shows as a change "via shell".
- A command run in the background is compared when it starts running in the background, not when it ends.
- Shell tracking pauses for the rest of the session, saying so once in the transcript, when a git snapshot
  takes over 2 seconds, when git does not answer within 3 seconds, or when the uncommitted changes are over
  4 MiB. File tools are still tracked.
- Up to 25 changed files are compared per command; the rest are counted in one "more files" step.
  A step draws at most 400 diff lines; a turn keeps at most 300,000 characters of diff and 500 steps.
  A step of very long lines (minified code) past 100,000 characters is cut by the pane and drawn without colour.
  Counts always cover the whole change.
- Arrow keys need a click on the "Keys" line first; without it, up and down step only on a step taller than
  the pane (the engine sends them as scroll keys only then). VS Code and the mobile app have no key line:
  use the buttons there. The band shows on the terminal and the desktop app only.
- File names with control characters are drawn with them replaced (ANSI sequences dropped, others shown as
  U+FFFD).
- A binary file's size is shown when git keeps the earlier copy (a delete or move); a new or changed binary
  in the working tree shows without it.
- `r` in the prompt box types an `r`; it presses Replay only once the band has the keyboard.

## Built from a prompt

This mod was built from [prompts/play-by-play.md](../../prompts/play-by-play.md).

# Porthole

A live preview of the app you are building, right beside the chat.

## Install

```
/plugin install porthole --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

| You type | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `/porthole http://localhost:5173` | Opens the Porthole pane with a screenshot of the page, sized to the pane. A site other than localhost opens only when you type the command yourself. |
| `/porthole` | Opens the last dev-server address porthole saw (or the page already in the pane). |
| `/porthole mobile` / `/porthole desktop` | Switches the viewport to 390 px or 1280 px wide and shoots again. |
| `/porthole 3000` or `/porthole localhost:3000/app` | Shorthands for a local address. |

`/porthole` runs at once even while Claude is working, so you can open or refresh the preview mid-turn.
When it works it says so in a toast and adds nothing to the conversation; a refusal (an address it will
not open, Chrome missing) stays visible as the command's output.

- **Dev-server detection.** When a Bash result from Claude names a local server
  (`http://localhost:<port>` or `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`), a toast says
  `Ready to preview http://localhost:5173/ - type /porthole` (Claude Code shows it under porthole's name). Each address is offered once per session.
  Only foreground Bash results are read: a server Claude starts in the background is offered once its log
  passes through a Bash result (for example `cat` of the log).
- **Auto refresh.** While the pane is open, a file edit by Claude (Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit)
  refreshes the screenshot 2 seconds later. Edits inside that window share one refresh, so refreshes are
  never closer than 2 seconds apart, and the dev server gets a moment to rebuild first. Only local pages
  refresh this way; a remote page you opened refreshes when you press `Refresh`.
- **In the pane.** A status line (address, viewport, shot number), a `Refresh` button and a
  `Mobile` / `Desktop` button. Close it with the pane's own close mark; that also deletes the picture.

## Settings

Every setting has a default, so the notice at install about options not yet set is expected; change them in `/config`.

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `chromePath` | empty | Full path to a Chrome or Chromium executable. Empty: porthole looks in `/Applications` (Google Chrome, Chromium) and then on `PATH` (`google-chrome`, `google-chrome-stable`, `chromium`, `chromium-browser`). |

## What it can touch

- **Processes.** For each screenshot: `mktemp -d` to make a private run folder in `$TMPDIR` (or `/tmp` when `TMPDIR` is unset or not an absolute path), then the Chrome
  you already have, headless:
  `--headless=new --disable-gpu --hide-scrollbars --no-first-run --no-default-browser-check --disable-extensions --disable-background-networking --disable-sync --use-mock-keychain --force-device-scale-factor=1 --timeout=15000 --user-data-dir=<run folder>/profile --window-size=W,H --screenshot=<run folder>/shot.png -- <url>`.
  Arguments are passed as a list, never through a shell. Chrome is stopped as soon as it reports the PNG
  written (30 second hard stop). `rm -rf` runs only on porthole's own run folders
  (`$TMPDIR/porthole.XXXXXX`, or `/tmp/porthole.XXXXXX` without an absolute `TMPDIR`, and the profile inside), checked by an allow-list before every call.
- **Browser profile.** A brand new profile every shot, deleted as soon as Chrome stops: no cookies, no
  signed-in accounts, nothing shared with your own Chrome.
- **Files and environment.** Checks that Chrome and the screenshot exist. Reads no project files. Reads
  the `PATH` and `TMPDIR` variables. The screenshot is read by the terminal itself to draw it.
- **Network.** Porthole itself makes no network calls. Chrome loads the page you asked for and everything
  that page loads in turn (scripts, fonts, images, API calls, which can be on other sites), and runs its
  JavaScript, as any browser would, once per screenshot. Headless Chrome itself may also make background
  requests of its own (component updates, safe browsing and similar), even for a localhost page: the
  flags above switch off the ones Chrome lets you switch off, but this is not verified to be zero.
- **Who may open what.** Porthole opens `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` on its own. Any other site opens only
  when you type `/porthole <full http:// or https:// URL>` yourself, at the terminal or through Remote
  Control. The same command arriving from anywhere else (another plugin, a peer session, a channel relay,
  a task notification, a schedule, an SDK script) gets localhost only and a one-line refusal. `file:`,
  `javascript:`, `data:`, `chrome:` and every other scheme are always refused.
- **Model calls.** None.

## Limits

- **Terminal only.** The picture is a terminal `Image` (kitty graphics protocol). The engine documents
  kitty and Ghostty; in a terminal it cannot draw in (or over ssh or tmux, where the terminal cannot read
  the file) the pane shows a text stand-in, a toast says so once, and auto refresh pauses. Manual refresh
  still works.
- **Desktop app, VS Code, mobile.** The pane shows one line pointing you to the desktop app's built-in
  browser pane, and porthole does not start Chrome there. (Commands typed in the desktop app likely arrive
  as SDK turns, which count as not typed by you; with no terminal there is no screenshot either way.)
- **A screenshot, not a browser.** You cannot click or scroll the page; you see its top. Pages behind a
  login show the logged-out view, by design of the throwaway profile.
- **The toast has no button.** Toasts in this API carry text only, so the toast names the command to type.
- **Detection reads Bash results only.** A server Claude starts in the background is caught when its log
  passes through a Bash result (for example `cat` of the log). Addresses like `0.0.0.0`, `[::]` or a LAN IP
  are not detected; type them in full.
- **Sizing.** The first shot after opening is 1280 x 800 (the pane has not been measured yet); later
  desktop shots match the pane's shape. Pictures are fitted assuming a terminal cell about twice as tall
  as it is wide.
- **macOS and Linux.** Uses `mktemp` and `rm`; Windows is not supported.

## Built from a prompt

This mod was built from [prompts/porthole.md](../../prompts/porthole.md).

# Redline

Context fill, session cost and pace on one line, with a warning before the red line.

```
ctx 82% ████████░░ RED · ≈$4.12 · 3.9k tok/min · full in ~7m · 5h 46% · 7d 13%
```

## Install

```
/plugin install redline --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

- **Status line** (under the prompt), updated on every model request:
  - context fill as a percentage with a 10-cell bar, and the level as a word: nothing under 60%, `AMBER` from 60%, `RED` from 80% (the status line has no colour, so the word carries it);
  - the session cost so far, marked `≈`: Claude Code's own estimate (what `/cost` shows) where it keeps one, otherwise redline's price table;
  - new tokens per minute over the last 10 minutes;
  - the pace: when the context hits 100% at the rate it grew over the last 10 minutes (`full in ~25m`);
  - your plan's 5-hour and weekly windows (`5h 46%`, `7d 13%`), with `out in ~40m` added when a window will run dry before it resets. A spent window says when it comes back (`5h OUT, resets in ~1h 20m`), and `5h reset` once that time has passed.
- **Toast at 80%**: one toast suggesting `/compact` or a fresh session (`/clear`), once per crossing. It re-arms only after the context drops under 75% (a compaction, a fresh session), so it never nags on every redraw.
- **`/redline`** opens the detail view in a pane, laid out to the collection's UI standard: a hero line with the context fill in its colour and the bar beneath; label and value rows (pace, throughput, tokens, cost, session, requests) with the figures at the right edge and the breakdowns dim beneath them; each plan window as a bar with its reset time and run-out; the five busiest turns; and one footnote for the caveats. The cost headline is Claude Code's own estimate (what `/cost` shows) when it keeps one, else the price table's, both marked `≈`. Rows that would read zero before the first request are not drawn. Buttons: show or hide the band, close. Where no surface places the pane, the same view goes to the transcript as dim rows of its own, which the model does not read.
- **`/redline spend`** opens the same pane for its **Where the money went** section: this session's cost split by the kind of work each model request carried, one row per kind (prompt, reading, editing, shell, search, planning, subagents, answering, an MCP server's tools by its name) with a share bar, the request count and the cache share, then the same by model. The rule, stated under the rows: a request is charged to the kinds of the tool results it carried (the previous reply's tool calls), split evenly when it carried several; a turn's first request is the prompt; a subagent's requests are subagents. Every figure is a list-price estimate, marked `≈`; nothing new is stored, and the band does not change.
- **`/redline band`** toggles a band above the prompt with the same gauge, in colour (green, amber, red), for people who hide the status line. Its `Hide` button turns it off. The choice is remembered across sessions. It shares the band: whatever other mods draw there stays, drawn first, with the gauge on the line after it. It steps aside while a survey holds that space.

## Settings

None. The thresholds (60%, 80%, re-arm under 75%) and the 10-minute window are fixed.

## What it can touch

- Reads: what Claude Code reports about the session (`$.session.usage()`, the `session.measure` event), each model request's token counts (`turn.step`), each turn's prompt text (`turn.start`, shown only in the busiest-turns list), and compactions, `/clear` and an in-session `/resume` (each starts the gauge over). Model ids, plan window names and prompt text are cleaned of control characters before anything is drawn.
- Writes: one remembered value in the plugin's own store (whether the band is on). No files.
- No processes, no network, no model calls. No tokens: nothing it draws reaches the model.

## Where the numbers come from

- **Context window**: Claude Code reports it for the model in use, so a 1M-token model reads correctly. No table is involved.
- **Context fill**: Claude Code's own figures (`context.tokens` and `context.percent`, the status line's used percentage) whenever it has measured the latest request. Between its measurements the gauge counts the main conversation's last request itself, input side (uncached + cache read + cache write), the same way, so it moves on every request. Subagent requests count toward tokens and cost, never toward the session's context.
- **Session cost**: Claude Code's own total (`cost.usd`, what `/cost` shows), labelled as its estimate and marked `≈`: it is summed at list prices over the session's responses, not a bill (on a subscription nobody pays it). Where Claude Code keeps no ledger, redline's built-in price table prices the requests it counted, and a model the table does not know shows tokens only, never a guessed price.
- **Price table** (`hooks/prices.ts`): list prices per model family as of 2026-10-08, used for the per-category and per-turn estimates. It leaves out long-context premiums, fast mode, 1-hour cache writes, batch and regional pricing, so every figure from it is marked `≈`.
- **Plan run-out**: the window's current rate, how far it moved over the last 15 minutes of readings, so a late burst warns even when the average looks calm. When it has not moved in that time, the average pace since the window opened (its reset time less its length) stands in; the detail view says which of the two it used. A gateway's spend limit gets an estimate only from its recent rate.

## Limits

- Plan windows appear only on a Claude subscription, after the first reply of a session; with an API key there are none, and the detail view says so.
- Token counts (and the price-table estimate) start when redline loads; Claude Code's cost estimate and the context fill cover the whole session. A plan window's recent rate needs readings from this session, so right after start the average stands in.
- The pace needs a minute of growing context inside the last 10 minutes. Flat or shrinking context gives no estimate. Right after a compaction the fill is Claude Code's own estimate of the compacted size until the next reply measures it.
- The status line, band and pane update on model requests and measurements, not on a timer. Two one-shot repaints are the exception: 10 minutes after the last reading (so an idle session stops showing a pace and rate) and just after each plan window resets (so a spent window flips to `reset` while you wait). The session time in the detail view refreshes with readings.
- Terminal and desktop are supported and tested. VS Code and mobile draw the pane through the same hooks but are not tested.

## Built from a prompt

This mod was built from [its prompt](../../prompts/redline.md).

- Animate only while the band is visible. Stop all timers when idle.

# Second Wind

A breath, an eye rest or a stretch while Claude works, sized to the wait.

## Install

```
/plugin install second-wind --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

Just work. When a turn has run for 3 seconds, a small band appears above your prompt. Quick turns never show it.

```
Breathe in 4  physiological sigh
──────────▐████████████████████▌──────────
```

- It opens with one **physiological sigh**: a deep inhale, a short top-up sip, a long slow exhale (15 seconds).
- If the turn keeps going, it moves into **slow paced breathing** (5.5 seconds in, 5.5 seconds out), or **box breathing** (4-4-4-4) if you pick it.
- On turns over 60 seconds it swaps in a **20-20-20 eye rest** ("Look at something 20 feet away" for 20 seconds) or a one-line **stretch** at the end of a breath, then goes back to breathing. Another comes every couple of minutes after that.
- In the terminal the words read the phase and count down (`Breathe in 4`, `Sip in 2`, `Hold 4`, `Out 6`), and a bar fills from the middle outward and empties with the breath. In the desktop app it is Bolt, eyes closed, in a soft halo that swells on the in-breath and settles on the out-breath, with the step's words fading beside him (`Breathe in`, `Sip in`, `Hold`, `Breathe out`) and the pattern's name after them. No countdown there: the drawing keeps its own clock.
- When Claude answers, the breath is not cut off: an exhale already under way runs out its own time, and an inhale turns into a closing exhale. Then the band folds into one line, dims and clears:

  ```
  4 breaths while Claude worked · 37 today · 6-day streak
  ```

- While you type your next prompt, the band shrinks to one quiet line. It also uses that one line when the space above the prompt is short, and it sizes itself to the width it is given (narrower beside a docked pane), drawing beneath anything other mods put in the band, so a tight band clips the breath, never another mod's prompt.
- The spinner's verb follows the breath (`Breathing in…`), but only when Claude Code is not showing a status of its own there.
- It only follows the main conversation. Subagents starting and finishing never restart or stutter the breath.

### Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/breathe` | Today's breaths, eye rests and stretches, your streak, all-time breaths and the current settings |
| `/breathe off` | Hides the band now and on every later turn |
| `/breathe on` | Brings it back |
| `/breathe snooze` | Off for the rest of today, back tomorrow |
| `/breathe card` | Copies a small text card of your stats to the clipboard to share |
| `/breathe help` | What it does, and the safety line |

`/breathe` runs at once, even mid-turn.

### Movement card (off by default)

Turn on `movementCard` and every fifth long turn offers a card above the prompt, "Stand up and stretch" or "10 squats", with **Did it** and **Skip** buttons (click one, or Tab to it and press Enter; there are no letter keys, so they never clash with other mods' buttons). It never blocks the prompt: keep typing and answer it whenever you like. It goes away when you press a button or start your next turn. **Did it** counts a move for today.

Breathe gently and never strain. If you feel lightheaded, stop and breathe normally.

## Settings

Change them in `/config`. Installing says these options are not yet set: each has the default below, so nothing needs setting first.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pattern` | `slow` | What follows the opening sigh: `slow` (slow paced breathing) or `box` (box breathing) |
| `motion` | `full` | `full` animates the shape; `gentle` moves it less and redraws twice a second; `still` shows the words only, for reduced motion |
| `delaySeconds` | `3` | How long a turn runs before the band appears (0 to 600) |
| `eyeRest` | on | Offer the 20-20-20 eye rest on turns over 60 seconds |
| `stretch` | on | Offer a one-line stretch on turns over 60 seconds |
| `movementCard` | off | Offer the movement card every fifth long turn |

## What it can touch

- **Store:** its own store keeps counts and dates only: breaths, eye rests, stretches and moves for today and in all, the day they belong to, the streak and its last day, how many long turns there were, and whether you turned it off or snoozed it (and which day).
- **Session state:** the breath in progress, the time it was last drawn, whether you are typing, and an offered card. Nothing of your prompt is kept: typing is read only as "the box is empty or not".
- **Clipboard:** only when you run `/breathe card`.
- **Commands:** `/breathe` writes its answer as a dim transcript note for you. Claude never reads it, so it costs no tokens.
- **Status line:** on mobile and in VS Code only, the current cue (see Limits).
- **Timers:** one, and only while a turn runs and something can show the band: 8 redraws a second for `full`, 2 for `gentle`, 1 for `still`. While the fold line shows it waits without ticking. Between turns no timer runs, and a run whose turn ended unseen stops at the band's next draw. In a plain `-p` run, or with no window or phone attached, it does nothing at all and counts nothing.
- **Files, processes, network, model calls:** none.

## Limits

- In the desktop app, a `/breathe` sent as the very first prompt of a new session may show "/breathe isn't a command here." The app checks the command before mods have registered theirs; the command still runs, and later ones show no such line.
- **Surfaces:** the band and the spinner are drawn by Claude Code in the terminal and the desktop app only. On mobile and in VS Code mods get neither, so there Second Wind puts the current cue in its status line instead, and only when no terminal or desktop window is attached to the session.
- **The desktop guide** is an SVG drawing in a frame of its own, so it uses Bolt's own colours (lime, with a lime halo at partial opacity) and follows the app's light or dark mode for the words; everything else uses your theme's colours. The desktop app loads that frame again whenever the band is drawn again, identical or not, which looked like flashing. So on the desktop the band is drawn once per stretch of breathing (about two minutes, until the next eye rest or stretch), and nothing beside the guide counts down. A draw that lands anyway (a draft cleared, a movement card, a resize) reloads the guide once, picking up where the breath is.
- **Days** are your computer's local calendar days. Flying west so the date goes back never breaks a streak.
- **Typing:** the band shrinks while the prompt box holds a draft and grows back when it is emptied or sent, in the terminal and the desktop app alike. It reads this from the hint line under the prompt, so it follows a beat after that line redraws.
- **Counts:** breaths count only for the turn that showed them. If a turn's end never reaches the mod (another mod held it, or a reload landed at that moment), that turn's breaths are dropped rather than added to the next turn. In the terminal and the desktop app its clock stops at once; on mobile or in VS Code alone it runs on until your next turn starts.
- **Reloads:** changing a setting reloads the mod. A breath already running keeps its old settings until the turn ends, and its animation resumes on the band's next draw.

## Built from a prompt

This mod was built from [`prompts/second-wind.md`](../../prompts/second-wind.md).

# Thermostat

Shows when your prompt cache goes cold, and stops the expensive send.

Claude Code keeps your conversation in a prompt cache. After a stretch of quiet (about an hour on a subscription, 5 minutes on an API key) the cache lapses, and the next message re-reads the whole conversation at the full cache-write price. Thermostat shows you that clock, holds the surprise send once, and can keep the cache warm while you are away when that is actually cheaper.

## Install

```
/plugin install thermostat --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

**The countdown.** At the end of the prompt footer, beside the mode labels:

- `cache warm · 41m left` - quiet while there is time
- `cache warm · 8m left` - amber in the last 10 minutes (the last 2 of a 5-minute window)
- `cache cold · 182k to re-read` - once it has lapsed
- `· warming 1h12m` is added while `/warm` runs

This draws on the terminal and the desktop app. Where no footer draws (VS Code, mobile, or a footer that is hidden) the same text appears on the plain status line under the prompt, without colour. Nothing shows until the conversation has something cached.

**The guard.** When you send a prompt on a cold cache, it is held once and you see what it costs:

> Cache went cold 23m ago: this send re-reads 150k tokens (~$1.20 vs ~$0.03 warm, Opus 5.5 API list prices).
> Send again to go ahead, or /clear to start fresh.

Send it again to go ahead (the words are put back in the prompt box if it is empty), or `/clear` to start a fresh conversation instead. It only holds prompts you type yourself (at the terminal, in the desktop app, or through Remote Control; never a headless `claude -p` run, where nobody would see the hold), only when the re-read is at least 20k tokens, never a prompt typed while a turn is running, and a hold counts as seen for 10 minutes.

**Keep-warm.** `/warm 90m` (or `2h`, `1h30m`, `45`) sends a tiny ping just before the cache would go cold, for as long as you asked. Before every ping it compares what the remaining pings will cost with what one cold re-read would add; if pinging costs more, it stops and says so in the transcript. It also refuses up front when the whole window would not pay. `/warm` on its own shows where it stands, `/warm off` stops it. Only a `/warm` you type starts or stops it; another plugin's command cannot. Confirmations appear as a toast; when it will not start, the reason stays in the transcript as a dim note. A window can run up to 24 hours.

How a ping works: it re-sends the conversation's last request (same model, system prompt, tools and messages) with one line asking for the word "ok", tools denied. That reads the conversation's own cache entry, which restarts its timer. Nothing is added to your transcript. Every ping's usage is checked: if it did not read the conversation back from the cache, keep-warm stops rather than keep paying for pings that are not helping.

**The receipt.** `/thermostat` opens a pane (a transcript note where no pane can be drawn, as in `claude -p`) laid out to the collection's UI standard: the cache right now as one line in its colour (`Warm · 41m left`, `Cold · 98k to re-read`), the window's bar and the next send's price beneath, Bolt beside them (asleep while the cache is cold or empty); then a row each, the figure at the right edge and the detail dim beneath, for cold sends paid (and how much more than warm they cost), prompts held (and how many you answered with `/clear`), keep-warm pings (what they cost, and the sends that arrived warm because of them), money saved, Claude Code's own estimate of the session's total cost (what `/cost` sums at list or managed prices, not your bill), and the guard; a figure still at zero draws no row. One footnote says what the dollars are.

## Settings

Every setting has a default, so the notice at install about options not yet set is expected; change them in `/config`.

| Field | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `guard` | `hold` | `hold` stops the first cold send once and shows the cost. `warn` shows the cost in a toast and sends. `off` does nothing. |
| `cacheMinutes` | `0` | The cache window in minutes, used until Claude Code reports its own. `0` works it out from your login. |

The window is worked out in this order: what Claude Code itself reports (its cache TTL on a model switch, or whether a resumed cache has expired), then `cacheMinutes`, then your login (60 minutes on a subscription, 5 on an API key), and 5 minutes when none of these is known.

Prices come from a small table of API list prices per model family (October 2026), with cache writes at 1.25x input for the 5-minute window and 2x for the hour. When Claude Code prices a re-cache itself (on a resume or a model switch, including an organisation's managed pricing), its rate is used instead. On a subscription the dollars measure how much of your plan a send uses, not a bill.

## What it can touch

- **Reads:** each prompt as you submit it (to decide whether to hold it; the text is not kept), the token counts of each main-conversation model request, what Claude Code reports on a resume or model switch, the prompt box (only to check it is empty before putting a held prompt back), which kind of login the session uses (the kind only: the credential stays with Claude Code, and this mod makes no network requests that could use it), and Claude Code's estimate of the session's cost.
- **Writes:** its own session state, the prompt box (a held prompt's words, only into an empty box), the footer label and status line, the receipt pane, toasts, and short dim notes in the transcript. None of these is sent to the model: `/warm` and `/thermostat` answer with no command output when you type them, so they cost no tokens. The only command text is a one-line notice when `/warm` is run by something other than you (keep-warm changes only with a `/warm` you type) and a one-line error notice if either command fails; neither carries any of your data. No files, no settings, nothing kept across sessions.
- **Processes and network:** none.
- **Model calls:** only keep-warm pings, only after you run `/warm`, at most one per cache window (about every 58 minutes on a subscription, every 4 minutes on a 5-minute window). Each costs roughly one cache read of the conversation plus a few tokens; the smart rule stops them as soon as they would cost more than they save, a window ends after 24 hours at most, and three failed pings in a row end it too.

## Limits

- The window is a model of the cache, not a reading of it. Claude Code only states its cache TTL on a model switch (and implies it on a resume), so until then it comes from your login or `cacheMinutes`. Other things can make a send cold early (tools or instructions changing, the cache being evicted); the receipt still books those from the real token counts.
- The countdown starts with the first model request after the mod loads, or with a resume. Installed in the middle of a conversation, it shows nothing until your next message.
- After a model switch the new model starts with nothing cached, so that first send is neither held nor counted as a cold send.
- A ping can make the model think, which is billed as output; the measured cost of each ping feeds the next decision. Pings cannot go out while the computer sleeps; if it sleeps past the expiry, keep-warm stops and says so.
- In the desktop app the held prompt may not go back into the prompt box (the app can refuse that); send it again from your history. The desktop app is recognised by its prompts arriving as an SDK host's with a desktop surface attached; prompts from the VS Code extension are not held.
- The guard puts a held prompt's words back into the prompt box (only when the box is empty); attached files are not put back.
- The footer label is checked through the engine's test kit on the terminal and desktop surfaces; how each terminal paints it has not been checked by hand.
- Prices are list prices unless Claude Code priced a re-cache itself. Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex AI bill separately.

## Built from a prompt

This mod was built from [the Thermostat prompt](../../prompts/thermostat.md).

# Wardrobe

Restyle Claude Code live, including colourblind-safe and high-contrast themes.

## Install

```
/plugin install wardrobe --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/wear` | Opens the gallery: a card per theme with a sample tool row drawn in that theme, its diff chips, Bolt in the theme's costume and a `wear` button; the one you wear is marked. Close it with its close mark or ctrl+x x. |
| `/wear <theme>` | Switches now. Rows still live on screen redraw in the new look, and the switch band shows the theme above the prompt for six seconds. |
| `/wear auto` | A day theme by day and a night theme by night (see Settings). |
| `/wear season` | The seasonal pack the calendar calls for, re-checked daily (see Seasonal packs). |
| `/wear pin` | This project keeps what it wears now; other projects keep the global choice. While pinned, `/wear <theme>` changes this project's pin. |
| `/wear unpin` | This project follows the global choice again. |
| `/wear <theme> --match` | Wears the theme and sets Claude Code's own `theme` setting (the `/theme` menu) to the built-in nearest it: a light look on a dark theme turns the theme light, keeping a daltonized or ansi variant. Your own theme is remembered. From the desktop app this changes the terminal's theme; the app keeps its own look. |
| `/wear match` | The same for the theme worn now. The gallery's `match theme` button does both at once. |
| `/wear default` | Back to Claude Code's own drawing. After a match, Claude Code's theme goes back to the one you had, unless you changed it yourself since the match: then your choice stands. |

Each command answers in a toast (an unknown theme's message stays longer). Nothing `/wear` says is added to the conversation, so it costs no tokens and never reaches the model.

Themes: `noir`, `paper` (light), `tokyo-night`, `dracula`, `catppuccin`, `solarized`, `nord`, `high-contrast`, `colorblind`, and the seasonal packs `halloween`, `christmas`, `spring` (light), `summer`, `autumn`. Short forms work too: `drac`, `hc`, `colourblind`, `tokyo night`, `xmas`, `fall`, `spooky`, and any prefix that names one theme alone (`sp` is spring, `su` is summer).

Every look also ships as a Claude Code theme file (`themes/<look>.json`), listed in `/theme` as "<Look> (wardrobe)". `--match` prefers it, so in the terminal the input box border, your message background, the text and the diff colours follow the look too; the desktop app keeps its own theme.

What changes, on the terminal and in the desktop app:

| Where | What wardrobe draws |
| --- | --- |
| Tool rows | A one-cell stripe in the theme's accent, the theme's icon for the kind of tool (shell, read, edit, write, search, web, agent, todo, MCP), Claude Code's own row, then a status glyph and, for a finished call, the time since Claude asked for it (any wait for your approval included). |
| Folded tool groups | The stripe, one icon per call before the count line; a failed call in the error colour. |
| Diff cards (Edit, Write) | Numbered lines in the theme's add and remove colours, with a `+N -N` summary. |
| Small shell output | A themed card; stderr lines are marked `!`, not only coloured. |
| Spinner | The theme's suffix after the word (never over Claude Code's own status message); on a terminal 60 columns or wider, a chip saying what the turn is doing (thinking, writing, using tools). |
| Turn duration | A themed `Baked for 3s` line (the terminal draws this line; the desktop has its own footer). |
| Above the prompt | The switch band, for six seconds after `/wear` (see below). |

### Seasonal packs

Five themes made for a time of year, each with its own mark and icons: `halloween` (pumpkin orange, violet and bone white on near-black, mark `☾`), `christmas` (holly green, berry red, snow white and gold on deep pine, `❄`), `spring` (a light theme: fresh green, blossom pink and sky blue on cream, `❀`), `summer` (sun yellow, sea teal and coral on deep navy, `☼`) and `autumn` (amber, rust, moss and cream on dark brown, `❧`). Every pair they paint meets the same 4.5:1 bar as the other themes.

`/wear season` picks one by the local date and is stored like `auto`: wardrobe re-checks the calendar once a minute, so the pack turns over at midnight on its own, and `/wear` names what it wears now and why.

| Dates | Wears |
| --- | --- |
| Oct 15 to Nov 1 | `halloween` |
| Dec 1 to Jan 6 | `christmas` |
| Jan 7 to the end of Feb | `nord` (the frost theme; the rest of winter has no pack of its own) |
| Mar 1 to May 31 | `spring` |
| Jun 1 to Aug 31 | `summer` |
| Sep 1 to Nov 30, Halloween aside | `autumn` |

### Bolt in costume

Bolt, the modmyclaude mascot, wears each theme: in the gallery beside every card, beside the line that names what is worn, and in the switch band. A costume is an accessory drawn over the sprite, never a change to it: a witch hat for `halloween`, a santa hat for `christmas`, a flower crown for `spring`, sunglasses for `summer`, a beanie for `autumn`, a cape and fangs for `dracula`, cat ears for `catppuccin`, a headband for `tokyo-night`, a fedora for `noir`, reading glasses for `paper`, a sun visor for `solarized`, a beanie with a pom for `nord`, a bow tie for `high-contrast`; `colorblind` leaves Bolt plain. Every costume takes at most three colours, all from the theme's own palette, keeps the antenna light clear (each hat has a notch around it), and never uses Bolt's own pink or blush. `tests/costume.test.ts` holds every one of those rules for every theme and pose.

### The switch band

For six seconds after `/wear <theme>` (and after `/wear auto` or `/wear season` resolves to a theme) a band above the prompt shows the switch: one row filled with the theme's background, carrying its mark, `wearing <theme>`, its five icons, and Bolt in the theme's costume at the right when the band is 60 columns or wider. It draws under any other mod's band, never while a survey holds the band, and goes away by itself. `/wear default` raises none.

### Accessibility

- `high-contrast`: every colour pair wardrobe paints is at least 7:1 (WCAG AAA).
- `colorblind`: added lines are blue and removed lines orange, never red and green; tool icons differ by shape (triangle, disc, diamond, square, cross, bars).
- Every other theme, the seasonal packs included: at least 4.5:1 (WCAG AA). `tests/themes.test.ts` checks every pair of every theme.
- Every theme gives each tool kind and each status its own glyph, so colour is never the only cue.
- Every coloured span is painted on the theme's own background, so the contrast holds whatever your terminal's background is.

## Settings

Every setting has a default, so the notice at install about options not yet set is expected. Set these in `/config`. A time wardrobe cannot read falls back to its default, and `/wear` names it.

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dayTheme` | `paper` | What `/wear auto` wears by day. |
| `nightTheme` | `tokyo-night` | What `/wear auto` wears by night. |
| `dayStarts` | `07:00` | When the day starts, 24-hour local time. |
| `nightStarts` | `19:00` | When the night starts. A day that crosses midnight (`20:00` to `06:00`) works. |

## What it can touch

- Its own store: the global choice, the per-project pins (keyed by the path of the folder the session started in), and, once you have matched a theme, the Claude Code theme you had before and the one it set, so `/wear default` can put yours back and can tell when you changed it since.
- For the session, in memory: each tool call's start and end time, for its row.
- Reads the project root, the attached surfaces, the clock, and Claude Code's own theme setting (the `/config` theme row) at session start, before a match and before a restore; it also notices when you change that setting.
- Writes Claude Code's theme setting only when you ask: `/wear <look> --match`, `/wear match` and the `match theme` button set it, and `/wear default` sets it back to the one you had. No files, no processes, no network, no model calls. It never refuses or changes a tool call: its tool hook only notes when a call starts and ends.

### What a look changes, and what it cannot

**It changes:** tool rows and folded groups, diff cards and small shell output, the spinner's word and suffix, the turn line, the switch band, your prompt rows, Claude's reply rows and command output rows (a stripe, and the look's background where it may paint), the `wearing <look>` label in the prompt footer, the `/wear` gallery, and, only when you ask with `--match` or the `match theme` button, Claude Code's own theme: in the terminal the input box border, your message background, the text and the diff colours then follow the look.

**It cannot change:** the desktop app's window frame, sidebar, input box, page background and fonts; Claude Code's own text colours inside the rows, which follow `/theme` unless you match it; the spinner's word, which keeps Claude Code's own colour; permission dialogs, errors, diffs over the size limits and long shell output, which Claude Code draws itself; the terminal emulator's background and font; VS Code and the mobile app; rows already printed on the terminal's main screen; and a light look's panels on a dark app, which stay stripe-only until the theme is matched.

## Limits

- It restyles what Claude Code lets a mod draw. Claude Code's own text keeps its colours: the tool's own row inside wardrobe's stripe, icon and status, Read and Grep results, the prompt, dialogs and the transcript all follow Claude Code's own `/theme`. Wardrobe styles around them (the stripe, the chips, the band, the gallery); pick a matching `/theme` for the same reading everywhere.
- Tool rows wrap Claude Code's own row instead of replacing it, so expanding a row and its output keep working.
- Claude Code draws these itself: errors, diffs over 120 lines or 8,000 characters, binary diffs, edits held for review, and shell output over 8 lines or holding a control character other than a colour code (a progress bar's carriage return, a bell, NUL).
- Untrusted text it draws (paths, diff lines, shell output, settings) is cleaned first: colour codes are dropped and any other control character shows as U+FFFD, since Claude Code refuses a drawing that holds one.
- Where another mod draws its own tool result or turn line, wardrobe steps aside and that drawing stands. Tool rows, tool groups and the spinner wrap whatever is beneath them.
- A pin belongs to the folder the session started in: a subfolder or a worktree of the same repo is pinned separately.
- On the terminal's main screen, rows already printed keep their look; new rows, and everything in the fullscreen view, follow `/wear`.
- VS Code and the mobile app are not restyled; `/wear` says so when one is attached.
- Where nothing draws a toast or a pane (a `claude -p` run), `/wear` writes its words and the list to the log instead.
- Auto mode and season mode check the clock once a minute, so a switch can land up to a minute late. A choice made in another session reaches this one the same way.
- The switch band is a plain row above the prompt: it never covers a safety hold or a survey, and Bolt is left out of it under 60 columns.
- Tool calls made before wardrobe loaded show no time, and a refused or failed call shows its status but no time.
- Not verified: the paint itself in a real terminal and in the desktop app. The tests check the drawn trees against each surface's rules, not pixels.

starters.title: Mod Maker
starters.tagline: Describe the feature you wish Claude Code had. Get a tested, installable mod.
starters.prompt:
Build me a Claude Code mod: [what you want to see or change, e.g. "a pomodoro timer in the status line that chimes when 25 minutes are up and asks if I want a break"].

How to build it
- Mods are new (Claude Code 2.1.287+). Use your plugin-authoring skill and read the types it points to before writing anything.
- Pick the right shape and tell me in one line which and why: a band above the prompt, a side pane, a status line entry, a toast, a sound, a slash command, or a hook on tool calls or prompts.
- Keep it small: only draw and do what I asked. No network calls, no model calls and no reading files it does not need, unless I ask for them.
- If it can block or change anything (a tool call, a prompt), make it fail safe: when the mod itself breaks, it should say so, not silently let things through or silently block me.

Prove it works
- Write tests for the main behaviour, including the UI on both the terminal and the desktop app if it draws anything.
- Run `claude plugin validate` and `claude plugin test` until both pass.

Then
- Load it in this session so I can try it, and take my changes in plain words.
- When I say it is good: copy it to a folder I keep, install it so it loads in every session, and tell me where it lives and how to turn it off.
- Finally, add a marketplace file so I can share it, and give me the one-line install command to send a friend.

starters.prompt:
Read the mod catalogue at https://github.com/modmyclaude/claude-code-mods (the README and the prompts folder), then help me pick the mods worth installing.

Check my setup yourself first
- My OS, my Claude Code version (mods need 2.1.287 or newer), whether I am in a terminal or the desktop app, my terminal width, and whether my terminal can show images. Ask me only about what you cannot check.

Then ask me three quick questions
- Do I use subagents? Do I run long sessions or step away mid-session? Do I share my screen or record demos?

Recommend
- A table: mod, yes / maybe / skip, and one line on why for my setup. Flag anything that will not run here.
- Group the yeses into packs: Safety, Cost, Visibility, Looks. Order them by what I would feel first.
- Give the exact install line for each pick.
- Suggest one custom mod idea tailored to how I work, and offer to build it with the Mod Maker prompt.

Rules
- Do not install anything until I say yes to each one. Mods run with my permissions.
